reGrounding.note: Not applicable in its literal form — this territory is prose+equations, not line-numbered verse, so there is no population of verse-line trailing numbers to test for multiples-of-5. Its METHOD (a measured null over a population of trailing numbers) was directly reused here: sequential-page-footer's 'run of consecutive integers, ~60^-6 under an i.i.d. null' and equation-number-trailing-parens both descend from the same discipline S3 names.

Not one of this territory's 4 required seeds, but directly touched and worth recording: Shakespeare's Venus and Adonis (pg100) carries marginal cumulative line numbers on a 4-line interval (multiples of 4), not 5 -- 256/294 (87.1%) of trailing numbers are exact multiples of 4, the rest off by +/-1 from stanza-break counting edge effects. Confirms the seed's underlying mechanism (a printer's/editor's lineation, not content) but the specific modulus is edition-specific, not always 5.

The trailing-multiple-of-5 line-numbering signature was measured directly on 3 Gutenberg-plaintext verse originals in this territory (Aeneid, Dante, Faust — 30,430 combined non-blank lines) and found ZERO times. S3 does not describe Gutenberg-plaintext verse; it remains untested-by-me (not re-refuted) for its original Wikisource evidence base (Martial/Homer/Pindar), which is outside this territory. Scope-narrowed to Wikisource-style scholarly apparatus specifically — see rule no-editorial-lineation-in-verse, whose detector still implements the original positive test unchanged so it can fire on Wikisource material.

Re-grounded on the ORIGINAL: la.wikisource's Martial Epigrammata wikitext marks every 5th verse line with an explicit {{r|{{safesubst:#invoke:Romanus|Arabic|BOOK}}.N|N}} citation template (confirmed in Liber I). On live_priors this yields 1212 of 1212 trailing line-numbers (100%) as multiples of 5; P(this many or more | independent p=1/5 null) is effectively 0. This is the edition's own explicit numbering scheme implemented in the source, not an extraction coincidence -- upgraded from a measured pattern to an explained mechanism.

Explicitly re-grounded per task instruction. GRETIL's trailing numbers are the work's own sequential chapter/pāda.sūtra or verse address (e.g. Pāṇini ends at 8,4.68; Yogasūtra ends at 4.34), incrementing by 1 per unit -- not an editor's every-5th-line insertion. Spot-checked final numbers across all 8 fetched works: none are multiples of 5 as a rule, and the generating mechanism (traditional textual address vs added line-count) is categorically different from S3's Wikisource examples. The surface pattern (number after text) exists; the S3 mechanism does not transfer.

rules.name: hard-wrapped prose (typesetter's rule)
rules.action: join-wrapped-blocks

learnedFrom.note: measured on live_priors extractions while folding the archons, 2026-09-28; re-grounded on originals by the swarm where a territory touched it

reGrounding.note: Body prose IS genuinely hard-wrapped/justified (confirmed visually on 19650003019 pp.6-13), consistent with S2's prose classification — but on this territory's Acrobat-Capture-OCR'd sub-corpus, the 'would the next word fit' computation S2 relies on is itself corrupted by isolated-letter-split's spurious internal spaces (a single word reads as several short tokens). S2's geometry test must be applied after normalizing/rejoining split tokens on this source family, or its line-fill arithmetic silently misfires. Not checked on the cleaner 1980s TMs.

Re-grounded on originals (not extractions): Middlemarch 88.2% conjunction, Pride & Prejudice 86.6% (both >>50%, correctly wrapped-prose); Leaves of Grass 6.3% (correctly not wrapped-prose). W is confirmed NOT a corpus constant (71/72/72/74-75 across 4 works), validating the seed's own per-text-P95 prescription. NARROWED: Frankenstein measures 49.2%, just under the '>half' bar -- a real near-miss showing the AND-gate can false-negative on dialogue/letter-heavy prose. Also newly confirmed: PG plain-text wrap never hyphenates a split word (0/28044 lines), which the seed did not state but which the detector's arithmetic silently depends on.

Re-grounded on original bytes and split into two independently-confirmed, more precise claims (now separate rules): (1) Italian verse's lowercase-continuation pattern is real and GENERALIZES to Latin verse (Aeneid), not Italian-only as originally stated — rule verse-sentence-case-lineation; (2) 'German prose continues on capitalised nouns' is real and precisely measured against a Spanish-prose null (7.6x elevated, z>99) — rule german-noun-capital-not-sentence-boundary. Both halves HELD under re-grounding; the original single-sentence framing is narrowed into two separately falsifiable, separately scoped rules with measured evidence in place of the original qualitative claim.

Not applicable by mechanism in this territory: GRETIL sutra/verse works are not print-width-wrapped continuous prose (S2's target); the phenomenon here is collapse-to-one-line from a missing separator, not reflow-to-fit-a-column. No GRETIL file in this territory exhibited S2's wrapped-block shape.

Re-grounded and extended beyond S2's prose-wrap-detection scope into VERSE lineation: measured on the true Gutenberg Aeneid original (65.2% lowercase line-starts) and cross-checked on Homer's Greek original (83.2%) that capitalization in classical verse tracks sentence grammar straight through the line break in BOTH languages, confirming letter case is not lineation evidence there either.

Applied S2's own wrap-detection formula to 6 heimskringla.no Eddukvæði poems on the ORIGINAL bytes: brokenFrac ranges 2.4%-22.2%, all correctly under the 50% 'wrapped' cutoff, so S2 does not misfire on this new verse genre (a genuine positive result, not just an absence of testing). But re-grounding also surfaced a scope issue the seed didn't state: MediaWiki-sourced prose paragraphs are stored as ONE long unwrapped line each (measured mean 337 chars, max 1641, in Gylfaginning) -- there are no 'interior lines' for S2's formula to test at all outside deliberately-lineated verse. S2 should be explicitly scoped to sources with genuinely pre-wrapped bytes (Gutenberg/PDF/OCR); it is not merely non-firing but UNTESTABLE for MediaWiki wikitext prose, and its only real work in a wiki-sourced corpus is distinguishing verse-lineation from (rare, not observed here) accidental wrap within verse itself.

S2's line-length-percentile-plus-open-ending geometric test remains necessary and was NOT refuted — it is still the only method that works on Ranke's own English sibling translation (Ashworth 1887), which shows zero of the disambiguating glyph. But re-grounding on the actual German original reveals a cheaper, non-geometric shortcut exists for THIS class of source: Fraktur German text (at least this edition, and plausibly the broader period convention) marks line-end wraps with a dedicated glyph (U+2E17 'Doppelbindestrich', 95.3% line-final, 46x above a computed per-document chance rate) that a plain ASCII hyphen mostly does not carry in the same text (only 69.6% line-final, and vastly rarer: 316 vs 2527 occurrences). Where this glyph is preserved by the OCR, 'is this hyphen a wrap-join' can be answered from the character alone, before ever computing S2's percentile geometry — geometry becomes the necessary fallback only for lines with no trailing hyphen-like character at all, or for source/OCR combinations (confirmed: the English translation; likely: any non-German OCR) that don't carry the marker. Practical recommendation for eoreader7: try the glyph-based check first when the source script is German/Fraktur-OCR'd, fall back to S2's geometric test otherwise.

Hard-wrap-prose geometry does not apply to this territory's sources: Wikipedia/Wikisource/Wikinews/legislation/factbook/catalogues are all semantic-paragraph HTML or JSON originally, never fixed-width-wrapped plain text at the source. Would need a structured-web source that genuinely originates as hard-wrapped text (none found) to test.

learnedFrom.note: measured on live_priors extractions while folding the archons, 2026-09-28; re-grounded on originals by the swarm where a territory touched it

reGrounding.note: Not specifically measured against this territory's modal paragraph indent; a typewriter first-line indent was seen informally (e.g. body paragraphs in 19660017568) but not quantified relative to a modal value.

Re-grounded on two originals: Leaves of Grass (modal=2, 74.9%; run-over lines at +4/+5) and Shakespeare's Sonnets (modal=0 for the quatrains across all 154 sonnets; +2 marks the closing couplet, 152-153/154, the one exception being the textually 12-line Sonnet 126). The seed's blanket claim 'Gutenberg verse two [leading spaces]' does NOT hold as a corpus-wide absolute: in the Sonnets the baseline is 0 and +2 marks a specific rhetorical unit (the couplet), not verse-in-general; in Whitman the baseline itself is 2. Only the RELATIVE reading transfers -- a level above a work's own modal indent marks local structure -- never the specific absolute delta. Also newly found: the same relative-indentation check fires on Middlemarch's PROSE body too (secondary bands from occasional inset quotations), so the boolean alone is a weak discriminator; the histogram is the real output.

The specific claimed constant ('Wikisource=1 space, Gutenberg=2 spaces') does not hold even within Gutenberg alone: of 3 Gutenberg verse originals measured, only Aeneid uses 2-space indent (99.98%); Dante and Faust both use 0-space indent (99.3-99.5%). The METHOD S10 recommends ('read indent relative to the work's modal indent') survives and is what rule leading-indent-is-per-edition now implements; the platform-level constant is narrowed away. S10's Wikisource-side claim (1 space) was not re-tested by me (outside this territory's originals) so is UNTESTED here, not refuted.

For zh.wikisource.org, the 'leading space' S10 attributes to editorial indentation is not indentation at all. Neither the wikitext nor the rendered HTML of any fetched original has any leading/trailing whitespace on a paragraph (both are flush; verified byte-for-byte on shiji-juan001 and bencao-caozhiyi). The observed spacing is fully explained by one mechanism, ws-zh-tag-boundary-space-join: the extraction inserts a space at (something very like) every HTML tag boundary, block or inline, uniformly. This produces BOTH leading and trailing spaces (not just leading, as S10 states), plus internal spaces around every inline span/link, plus lone-space blank lines. Reading it as 'the edition's own indentation, relative to a modal value' would be actively misleading here: the modal value is 1 almost everywhere (measured 49.6% of all line-edges in shiji.txt), carrying zero discriminative structural information. This refutes the Wikisource-Chinese instantiation of S10 specifically; the seed's broader claim may still hold for other sources (e.g. genuine Gutenberg verse indentation), which is out of this territory's scope to test.

Re-grounded with two distinct findings. (1) In 6 of 8 works, all 12 'leading-space' lines sit at byte-identical relative positions strictly within GRETIL's fixed header boilerplate (confirmed by comparing line numbers against the '# Text' marker) -- pure furniture, not a body convention. (2) In Yogasūtra-with-bhāṣya, 153 leading-space BODY lines were confirmed present verbatim in the TEI's own literal text (e.g. the inset invocatory verse '<l>  yas tyaktvā rūpam ādyaṃ...'), a genuine encoder convention marking inset/quoted verse within prose commentary -- HELD in the strong sense of 'indentation is the edition's before it is the author's,' verified on the original, not introduced by any fetch step.

The work-wide baseline indent S10 describes is real but is only ONE of two distinct indentation phenomena in this territory: Homer's verse also carries a separate, MINORITY, colon-triggered extra indent (poem-colon-indent-marker) layered on top of whatever the modal baseline is, which must not be conflated with S10's blanket per-line indent.

No verse content in structured-web to test relative-indentation-as-edition directly. A conceptually related but domain-different echo was found in US Code: some USC subsections carry NO stored (a)/(1)/(A) label at all, only a CSS indent-level (role="listItem" class="indent1"), meaning position/indentation IS the only structure the edition (there, the USLM XML) provides — same underlying principle (indentation belongs to the edition, read it positionally, don't assume a label exists) applied to a structured-legal rather than verse context. Logged as a cross-domain resonance, not a direct test of S10 itself.

rules.name: The fraction of OpenCV-detected boxes carrying real OCR text mechanically separates a form/flowchart page from a chart or line-art page
rules.scope: pages already run through eoreader7's visual-detect.py; directional, based on 3 rendered pages (1 form, 2 graphics) in this pass
rules.statement: Once visual-detect.py has produced a box list for a rendered page, the fraction of boxes carrying non-empty OCR text tells forms apart from data graphics with no vision-model call. Measured: the Report Documentation Page (19880012630 p20) yielded 19 boxes, 19/19 text-bearing (fraction 1.00). A multi-curve gridded line chart (19660017568 p10) yielded 12 boxes, 0/12 text-bearing (fraction 0.00) — the detector is finding the chart's own gridline-bounded cells, not text regions. A single line-art diagram (19660017568 p26) yielded 1 box, empty (the whole figure's bounding contour). Every graphic page checked had fraction 0; the one form page checked had fraction 1. Two data points on the graphic side is a small sample — the exact boundary should be treated as directional, not precision-measured, until more graphic pages are checked.
rules.action: once a page has been through visual-detect.py for any reason, use this cheap post-hoc check to route it: high text-fraction routes to direct field parsing; low/zero text-fraction with many small boxes routes to treating it as a gridded chart (read via tesseract TSV or axis-aware methods, not per-box text); a single large empty box routes to treating it as a line-art diagram needing a genuine visual description, not per-region OCR
rules.port: pending — a reference detector held under falsification; to be expressed as an organ primitive + table before the organ runs it
rules.narrowedScope: The fraction-of-text-bearing-boxes heuristic only applies once visual-detect.py's mechanical box-finder returns >=3 boxes for a page at all, which does not reliably happen for an ordinary line/scatter plot without filled gridlines or a busy interior. The original two 'graphic' examples likely worked because their specific rendering (gridline-bounded cells; a single bounding contour) happened to produce a countable box set, not because graphic pages generally do.

rules.name: Hard-wrapped prose vs. intentional verse lineation
rules.scope: Reliable for descriptive/narrative English prose (85-90% conjunction observed); weakens toward the 50% decision line for dialogue- or letter-heavy prose, where short interjection- or salutation-final lines lack the closing punctuation the test expects even though they are still wrap artifacts.
rules.statement: A block is hard-wrapped prose when, for over half its interior lines, the next word would not fit at the text's own P95 interior line width AND the line does not end on closing punctuation. W is measured per text, not assumed, because it varies by edition.
rules.action: Rejoin interior lines of a fired block into logical sentences before any word-level reading; leave a non-fired (verse) block's line breaks alone.
rules.port: pending — a reference detector held under falsification; to be expressed as an organ primitive + table before the organ runs it
rules.narrowedScope: Conjunction-test reliably fires (>85%) for descriptive/narrative prose and correctly does not fire for verse (confirmed independently on 2 new works each). It becomes an unreliable coin flip -- and can wrongly call real hard-wrapped prose 'not-wrapped-prose' -- specifically on letter/dialogue-heavy prose, exactly the narrower zone the rule's own docstring already predicts. Separately, the auxiliary hyphenatedLineBreaks counter (not the fired-gate itself) is shown to be an unreliable measurement: on an Elizabethan text using '--' as em-dash punctuation, it overcounts genuine wrap-hyphenation by roughly 45x.
rules.counterexample: Frankenstein (real, unambiguously hard-wrapped epistolary prose) reproducibly scores 49.4% conjunction and is classified 'not-wrapped-prose (verse or too-short sample)' -- a real prose work misread as not-prose. Separately, pg811.txt has 46 lines the detector flags as hyphenatedLineBreaks, but manual inspection of them shows the overwhelming majority (e.g. "...great Lucifer;--" / "Is't not midnight?--come...") are '--' em-dash punctuation, not word-splitting hyphenation; the one apparent genuine hyphen ("FOUR-AND-" / "TWENTY YEARS") is itself a pre-existing compound-numeral spelling ('four-and-twenty'), not a wrap-inserted split -- so the counter's claimed signal (0 real wrap-hyphenations in PG prose) may still be technically true, but the /-$/ regex used to support it cannot tell the difference and is not a trustworthy measurement of it.

rules.name: Indentation is relative to a work's own modal indent, and its meaning is local
rules.scope: The rule's mechanism (find modal, flag any level >=3 above/below it as a candidate structural band) is a WEAK discriminator by itself: any sufficiently long real text will incidentally contain a few inset lines and will fire. The valuable output is the histogram/positional breakdown, which must be read against what kind of block it is -- not the boolean alone.
rules.statement: The specific number of leading spaces carries no fixed meaning across works; only the relation 'this band sits above/below this work's own modal indent' transfers. What the raised band marks (a run-over line, a couplet, an inset quotation) must be determined per work.
rules.action: Read the histogram, not just the boolean; treat a level above modal as a candidate structural marker to be interpreted per work, never as a corpus-wide constant.
rules.port: pending — a reference detector held under falsification; to be expressed as an organ primitive + table before the organ runs it
rules.narrowedScope: The 'read the histogram, the boolean alone is weak' guidance holds (confirmed concretely: Hiawatha's only secondary band turned out to be table-of-contents front matter, not verse structure -- exactly the kind of misleading positive the rule warns about). But the underlying mechanism (count literal leading ASCII-space characters) is tied to sources that encode indentation as characters. It does not transfer to a source that encodes the IDENTICAL text's indentation via markup/CSS instead of characters, even though the rule's own held-out prediction assumed it would.
rules.counterexample: PG's own transcription of Whitman's 'Song of Myself' carries a real, documented secondary indent band (the rule's own grounding data, +4/+5 = run-over lines). The identical poem, full text (1335 non-blank lines), pulled from Wikisource's own semantic wiki-markup (indentation there is CSS text-indent/margin-left plus <span class="ws-poem-indent"> spacers, not leading space characters -- confirmed by inspecting the raw HTML), shows a flat histogram: 1336/1336 lines at indent=0, no secondary level reaches even n=1. The held-out prediction ('same work, different source... expect fire') did not hold.

rules.name: Recurring ALL-CAPS period-terminated short line marks a drama speaker cue
rules.scope: English drama typeset in PG's plain-text convention. <=3 words and >=20 recurrences are hand-set thresholds (justified in the detector, no natural content-null exists for name length/recurrence) -- the raw counts are always returned so a caller can apply a different bar.
rules.statement: A short (<=3 words), ALL-CAPS, period-terminated line recurring at least ~20 times is a character/role cue, not a heading or an interjection.
rules.action: Use the qualifying candidate set as the play's character-name index; anything below the recurrence bar needs a second look, not automatic inclusion.
rules.port: pending — a reference detector held under falsification; to be expressed as an organ primitive + table before the organ runs it
rules.counterexample: pg811.txt (Doctor Faustus) genuinely contains hundreds of real speaker turns -- e.g. line 666: "FAUSTUS. Settle thy studies, Faustus, and begin" -- but this PG transcription places the speaker cue and the first line of dialogue on ONE shared physical line, mixed-case throughout. The detector requires the entire trimmed line to be uppercase letters only, so it never isolates a single real in-scene cue: qualifyingCount=0 despite FAUSTUS alone speaking dozens of times. The rule's scope ('English drama typeset in PG's plain-text convention') treats this as one convention; empirically at least two incompatible PG drama layouts coexist in the same corpus (Shakespeare's Complete Works isolates cues on their own line; this Marlowe transcription does not), and the detector only recognizes the first.

rules.name: Quote-character style is per-file, and U+2019 is genuinely overloaded
rules.scope: Quote/apostrophe character choice in this corpus tracks the transcription house/credits, not a corpus-wide PG constant. Ambiguity measurement only runs when curly quotes dominate (>=10 U+2019 occurrences).
rules.statement: Most David-Widger-credited PG texts use curly Unicode quotes almost exclusively; a Distributed-Proofreaders-credited text can use straight ASCII instead -- check per file, don't assume. Within a curly-quote file, U+2019 serves both as an apostrophe (contraction/possessive) and a closing single-quote; local-context classification (letter-before+letter-after = contraction; letter/punct-before + whitespace/quote-after = closing quote) is required.
rules.action: Measure the file's own curly-vs-ascii dominance before picking a quote-handling strategy; never hard-code U+2019 as purely an apostrophe or purely a closing quote.
rules.port: pending — a reference detector held under falsification; to be expressed as an organ primitive + table before the organ runs it
rules.narrowedScope: The core claims (style is per-file, don't assume; U+2019 is genuinely ambiguous and needs local-context classification) hold and are strengthened by new evidence. But the specific numbers cited as the expected range for the ambiguity split (3.2%-11.2% closing-quote-shaped, from 3 grounding texts) are not a safe bound -- a new target reaches 43.2%. The 'Widger=curly vs DP=ascii' causal story is also incomplete: a third, unrelated transcriber credit also produces ASCII.

rules.name: English title abbreviations defeat naive period-based sentence segmentation, and capitalization can't rescue it
rules.scope: English narrative prose. Presence is near-universal (even lyric verse and a style manual clear a low count) -- the useful signal is magnitude by genre, not a clean presence/absence split.
rules.statement: A period after Mr./Mrs./Dr./St./etc. is not a sentence boundary, but the word following it gives almost no signal to tell the two apart: both a genuine sentence-final period and a title-abbreviation period are followed by a capital letter essentially all the time in English. A closed-list lookup (a table, not a regex heuristic) is required.
rules.action: Subtract the closed-list-matched periods from any naive sentence-boundary count before trusting it; do not rely on the following letter's case.
rules.port: pending — a reference detector held under falsification; to be expressed as an organ primitive + table before the organ runs it
rules.narrowedScope: The core mechanism (title-abbreviation periods are not sentence-final; local capitalization cannot discriminate; a closed list is needed) holds fully. But 'presence is near-universal in English prose of any real length... even a lyric poem... clears the bar' overclaims: the true precondition is social-address narrative FICTION specifically. Three new, large, non-fiction/non-domestic English prose-or-verse works, none short, all fail to clear even the low minCount=5 bar.
rules.counterexample: A full, substantial (215KB) English narrative poem (Hiawatha) and a full formal historical-legal document (the Declaration of Independence) both score essentially zero (1 hit each), and Elizabethan drama (Faustus, 167KB) scores 4 -- all below minCount=5 -- directly contradicting the framing that any English prose of real length will clear the bar. Genre (domestic/social-address fiction), not length, is the actual driver.

rules.name: This corpus's live_priors ingestion strips PG's banner and nothing else
rules.scope: This specific live_priors gutenberg-en ingestion pipeline, verified on 4 works only. Does not generalize to other territories in the same live_priors tree (the seed file documents heavy corruption on Wikisource/GRETIL/scanned sources) and is not claimed for every Gutenberg file live_priors holds.
rules.statement: The extraction's only transformation is: strip PG's metadata header + START banner + END banner + license footer, trim leading/trailing blank lines, drop the final trailing newline. Every wrap, every _italic_ underscore, every CRLF, every indentation is carried over byte for byte.
rules.action: Trust this pipeline's byte-level fidelity for the 4 works checked; re-verify per new work before extending the trust claim, especially for any file whose banner or frontmatter looks inconsistent with its neighbors.
rules.port: pending — a reference detector held under falsification; to be expressed as an organ primitive + table before the organ runs it
rules.narrowedScope: The core transformation claim (strip banner/license, trim edge blanks, otherwise byte-identical) is reconfirmed exactly on 2 brand-new real works once paired by actual content. It is not a universal guarantee across time or across the whole live_priors tree: (1) a fresh re-fetch of a work already in live_priors can legitimately differ by a handful of lines due to Project Gutenberg's own later errata corrections, not extraction-pipeline fault; (2) at least one file in the same directory was never run through the strip pipeline at all.
rules.counterexample: Of 21,928 body lines compared between a fresh 2026-09-28 fetch of pg2701 and live_priors' 2026-08-03 snapshot, exactly 3 differ: "...Thy country? What people?' But mark now" (fresh) vs "...Thy country? What people? But mark now" (snapshot, closing quote mark dropped); a second dropped closing curly-quote; and "of my soul!" (fresh) vs "of my soil!" (snapshot) -- a genuine word-level difference most plausibly explained by Project Gutenberg applying a small errata fix to its live text between the two fetch dates, not by any fault in the strip transform. Separately, live_priors/01-literature-books/gutenberg/pg345_Dracula.txt is a complete, unstripped raw PG file (full header and license footer intact) -- a pipeline-coverage gap distinct from a stripping-fidelity defect.

rules.name: Catch a wrong Gutenberg id baked into a filename, at ingestion time
rules.scope: Must run on a FRESH original that still carries its PG header (before stripping) against the id/title the caller intended. Cannot recover an id from an already-stripped body.
rules.statement: A fresh PG original's own [eBook #N] and Title: fields are ground truth; compare them to what a filename/catalog claims before filing or citing the fetch.
rules.action: Run this on every fresh Gutenberg fetch before filing it; on fire, re-derive the correct id from the actual header and relabel/re-cite rather than trusting the intended id.
rules.port: pending — a reference detector held under falsification; to be expressed as an organ primitive + table before the organ runs it
rules.narrowedScope: The rule correctly flags every genuine wrong-id/wrong-title pairing it was tested against (12/12 true positives, 0 false negatives, across a full fresh 24-entry sweep) and is far more validated than its own sibling rule's 'one real defect' framing suggests. But the idMismatch half of the check is structurally unable to fire under the realistic 'fetch by id, then verify' calling pattern (actualId is parsed from the very file that URL-id was used to fetch, so it trivially always equals claimedId) -- in this entire run, 100% of real detections came from the fuzzy title-string comparison alone, which also threw 2 false alarms on exactly-correct id/content pairings whose canonical PG title merely differs in wording from the claim.
rules.counterexample: Across the 24-row sweep, idMismatch is false on every single row -- including the 12 rows with a completely different real book behind the id -- because actualId is read back out of the very original that was fetched using claimedId as the URL path segment, making that comparison a tautology in this (and, per live_priors' own fetch-gutenberg.mjs, apparently also the original ingestion's) calling pattern. All real detection work is done by normalizeTitle's substring-containment check, which also fires on id=100 ('Complete Works of Shakespeare' vs actual 'The Complete Works of William Shakespeare') and id=55201 ('by' vs 'of') even though both ids are exactly correct.

rules.name: Text-only illustration-tag count predicts presence, not always the exact file count, of images a CV look would find
rules.scope: PG works that ship BOTH a plain .txt and an illustration-aware -images.html (no page-scanned PDF/image layer was available for this territory within the polite-fetch budget, so pdftotext/tesseract/OpenCV were not applicable here -- see notes).
rules.statement: The '[Illustration' placeholder count in the plain text reliably predicts WHETHER interior images exist (0 tags means nothing but possibly a cover/logo), but does NOT always predict the exact count once real illustrations exist -- a paired-file (duotone) rendering technique and undocumented decorative dingbats can both break an exact match. This falsification is kept as the finding, not patched away.
rules.action: Skip a CV/page-image call when the tag count is 0 (treat a lone cover/logo as still-zero content images); once illustrations are present, budget 'on the order of N', not exactly N, and expect the file count to run slightly ahead of the tag count.
rules.port: pending — a reference detector held under falsification; to be expressed as an organ primitive + table before the organ runs it
rules.narrowedScope: The pure zero-tag-predicts-zero-image case holds (3/3 across the corpus, now including a reconfirmed Frankenstein). Any nonzero tag count cannot be trusted for exact count (now 2/2 real nonzero cases wrong, in BOTH directions -- P&P undercounts, Alice overcounts) nor, in Alice's case, even for 'at least one real interior image' -- because the cover/decorative-image exclusion is applied asymmetrically (only on the HTML side, never on the text's own '[Illustration' count). Applied outside its stated PG-txt/-images.html pairing (fed an unrelated non-PG source with no ctx.imagesHtml), the zero-case heuristic is evidentially vacuous: it 'predicts no images' for any source that simply doesn't use PG's own placeholder string, whether or not that source actually contains images.
rules.counterexample: pg11.txt's single '[Illustration]' tag (line 29) is the cover placeholder, and pg11-images.html's single is images/cover.jpg -- correctly excluded by the HTML-side cover regex, leaving htmlNonCoverImgCount=0 against a text count of 1. This is the mirror image of the already-documented pg37134/logo.png gap: there the HTML side kept an uncaught decorative image; here the TEXT side has no equivalent cover-exclusion, so a book with truly zero interior illustrations still reads as a text/HTML count mismatch.

rules.name: A corpus file's id/filename must never be trusted as its identity
rules.scope: Any Project Gutenberg plaintext etext, any language, fetched via the cache/epub convention; detector relies on Gutenberg's own header format (Title:/Author:/Language: fields, or the 'The Project Gutenberg eBook of <TITLE>' opening line, or the '*** START OF THE PROJECT GUTENBERG EBOOK <TITLE> ***' marker), all present since the mid/late-1990s convention this corpus uses.
rules.statement: A live_priors filename or manifest entry claiming 'this is work W, id N' must be verified against the FETCHED TEXT's own self-declared Title:/Author:/Language:, never assumed from the filename. Measured directly: 7 of 19 ids checked in and around this territory (36.8%) do not match their claimed work at all — not a subtle extraction artifact but a total content swap (e.g. id 2636 claimed as Goethe's Faust is Rafael Sabatini's English 'Historical Nights' Entertainment'; id 42671 claimed as Nietzsche's Zarathustra is Jane Austen's Pride and Prejudice). The errors cluster by corpus SHELF (see comparisons), not uniformly at random.
rules.action: Before reading a file for content, run this check; if fired, do not proceed to structural analysis under the assumed identity — surface the actual declared Title/Author/Language and treat the file as needing re-identification (or re-fetch under its real id).
rules.port: pending — a reference detector held under falsification; to be expressed as an organ primitive + table before the organ runs it

rules.name: A derived sidecar's recorded hash/byte-count must match the CURRENT source file
rules.scope: Any live_priors *.eot.json (nested source.sha256/source.bytes) or *.structure.json (top-level bytes) sidecar paired with a *.txt source in this corpus; generalizes to any pipeline that caches a derived reading next to a source file.
rules.statement: If a sidecar's recorded sha256 (or, absent a hash, its recorded byte count) does not match the CURRENT source file on disk, the sidecar was computed from bytes that no longer exist there: its line/unit counts and offsets are stale and must be re-derived, never trusted at face value. Measured: 10 of 10 sidecars checked in this territory (3 .eot.json + 7 .structure.json) were stale — 100%. The .eot.json mismatches were drastic (up to 19.6x byte difference), consistent with a wrong-book swap at some earlier pipeline stage; the .structure.json mismatches were small and uniform (1.2%-4.4% short), consistent with being computed before a later re-fetch/completion of the same, correct text.
rules.action: Never reuse a cached line count, offset, or unit boundary from a sidecar whose sha256/bytes do not match the current file; re-derive it from the live text instead.
rules.port: pending — a reference detector held under falsification; to be expressed as an organ primitive + table before the organ runs it
rules.narrowedScope: The core mechanism -- a sidecar's recorded hash/bytes not matching the CURRENT source file means the sidecar is stale and must be re-derived -- holds unconditionally and generalizes far past this territory (verified on 824 pairs across the whole live_priors corpus, plus a fresh self-consistency check and a deliberately-corrupted-hash sanity check). What does NOT generalize is the descriptive statistics offered as evidence: real corpus-wide drift is ~27%, not 100%; and drift magnitude does not cleanly split by sidecar schema (eot.json=drastic vs structure.json=small-and-uniform) the way the rule states -- roughly half of all drifted structure.json sidecars sit at a large ~1.8-1.95x ratio (a likely systematic doubling event on those shelves), and at least one drifted eot.json sidecar is modest (0.79x). Treat the '10 of 10 / 100%' figure and the drastic-vs-small dichotomy as anecdotal to the sample checked, not as a corpus-wide law.

rules.name: A transcriber's note declares this file's own emphasis/typeface symbols — read it, don't assume a default
rules.scope: Any Gutenberg etext (any language) carrying a 'Transcriber's note' / 'Anmerkungen zur Transkription' style preamble; re-grounds seed S17.
rules.statement: Some Gutenberg etexts declare, in a short preamble, what a bracketing ASCII character means for THIS file (asterisks = gesperrt/letter-spaced emphasis, tilde = a different typeface, underscore = italics, caret = superscript, …). This must be parsed per file and applied only to that file: measured directly, of the 14 originals in this territory only ONE (pg60360) declares the */~ = gesperrt/other-typeface convention verbatim ('Umschließungen mit * zeigen "gesperrt" gedruckten Text an, Umschließungen mit ~ Text, der im Original in einer anderen Schriftart dargestellt war.'), and a SEPARATE, unrelated file (pg42671) declares a DIFFERENT pair (underscore=italics) in the same note format — proving the declaration is per-file, not a corpus-wide constant. A naive /gesperrt/i search is a measured trap: pg7203, pg7204, pg7205 and pg2229 each contain the bare substring 'gesperrt' exactly once, every time as part of an ordinary German word (eingesperrt/abgesperrt/aufgesperrt = imprisoned/barred/unlocked), none of them a real declaration.
rules.action: If fired, use evidence.declarations' (symbol -> meaning) map to parse emphasis/typeface spans in THIS file; if not fired, do not assume any particular symbol convention for markup in this file.
rules.port: pending — a reference detector held under falsification; to be expressed as an organ primitive + table before the organ runs it
rules.narrowedScope: The rule's own core claims (per-file, non-corpus-wide declarations; the bare-'gesperrt'-substring trap) all reconfirm cleanly on original bytes I checked myself. But the detector's positive-detection is narrower than the rule's stated principle implies: it only catches a declaration when the literal glyph and its meaning-word share one clause. pg42671's own note -- the rule's own cited evidence file -- contains a second, real, human-readable declaration (caret = superscript, demonstrated by 'M^{rs}') that the detector silently misses because of hard-wrap-induced clause splitting. So fired=false must be read as 'no co-located declaration found', never as proof the file declares nothing.

rules.name: Classical/Romance verse capitalises a line only when it also starts a sentence
rules.scope: Italian and Latin verse editions in this bench (re-grounds and GENERALIZES seed S2 beyond its original Italian-only claim). Explicitly does NOT extend to German verse-drama, which is the measured contrast case.
rules.statement: In these editions, a verse line's first letter is capitalised if and only if it also begins a new sentence (the preceding line ends in terminal punctuation); an enjambment/continuation line stays lowercase. Measured on ORIGINAL bytes: Dante P(upper|after non-terminal)=3.75% (n=9304) vs P(upper|after terminal)=69.0% (n=5237), z=84.8; Aeneid P(upper|non-terminal)=10.8% (n=6409) vs P(upper|terminal)=79.1% (n=3522), z=68.3. Contrast: Faust (German verse-drama) shows almost no such gap — P(upper|non-terminal)=97.1% (n=2298) vs P(upper|terminal)=99.7% (n=3657), a 2.6-point gap versus Dante/Aeneid's 65-68 point gap — so this is not a general 'verse' property, only a Romance/classical sentence-case-lineation convention.
rules.action: When fired, use terminal punctuation on the PRECEDING line (not line-initial capitalisation) as the sentence-boundary signal for this verse text; when not fired, line-initial capitalisation may still carry its ordinary (line-boundary-independent) signal.
rules.port: pending — a reference detector held under falsification; to be expressed as an organ primitive + table before the organ runs it
rules.narrowedScope: Two corrections to the stated scope. (1) The boundary is not 'Romance/classical vs. German': it is the RENDERING language's own verse convention. Italian, Latin, and a Spanish translation of Goethe's own play all show the big sentence-case gap; an English original epic (Milton) and an English translation of that same German play both show a near-zero gap like the German source -- so the real split found is Romance-language verse vs. Germanic-language verse (English patterns with German, not with Romance), which the proposer never tested. (2) The statistic is not specific to verse at all: ordinary prose in Spanish, French, and German all clear the exact same fire threshold, so 'fired=true' alone cannot distinguish deliberate sentence-case verse lineation from a plain hard-wrapped prose file in a language that doesn't habitually capitalize nouns or every line.

rules.name: German hard-wrap capitals are routine noun-capitalisation, not sentence-boundary evidence
rules.scope: German prose (re-grounds the other half of seed S2). Contrast baseline measured on Spanish prose in the same bench.
rules.statement: Because German capitalises every common noun wherever it falls, a hard-wrapped continuation line beginning with a capital letter is routine and carries almost no sentence/clause-boundary information — unlike Spanish, where a line-initial capital at a wrap point is rare. Measured: P(capital at a >=45-char, non-terminal-ending wrap continuation) = 30.9% for Nietzsche's Jenseits von Gut und Böse (n=5368) and 32.5% for Der Wille zur Macht (n=8545), against a measured Spanish-prose null of 4.07% (Don Quijote, n=24687) — roughly 7.6x the null, z=99.3 and z=133.2 respectively. Concrete example from the original bytes: '...irgend ein' / 'Wortspiel vielleicht...' — 'Wortspiel' (a pun) is a common noun capitalised purely by German orthography at a line start that is mid-sentence, not mid-quote or a proper name.
rules.action: When fired, drop capital-letter-at-continuation as sentence-boundary evidence entirely for this text; rely on terminal punctuation and/or finite-verb position instead.
rules.port: pending — a reference detector held under falsification; to be expressed as an organ primitive + table before the organ runs it
rules.counterexample: pg135 (Les Misérables, Hapgood's English translation): 37,117 sampled hard-wrap continuations, 6.27% capitalised, z=21.4 against the Quijote-derived null of 4.07% -- 'fires' under this detector despite being ordinary 19th-century English prose with zero connection to German. Alice's Adventures in Wonderland (7.21%, z=6.18) and Sabatini's Historical Nights' Entertainment (7.78%, z=15.49) fire the same way. The single-Spanish-text null and a fixed z=5 gate cannot absorb the real variance across ordinary English prose, so 3 of 12 tested English works falsely cross the same bar the rule uses to claim German-specificity.

rules.name: A bare » opening a paragraph continues the previous speech, it is not an unterminated quote
rules.scope: This Quijote edition (pg2000/pg2000-body, and by extension any Spanish narrative prose using the same convention); a genuinely new finding, not a seed re-grounding.
rules.statement: Dialogue in this edition opens with a paragraph-initial em-dash (raya); when a single speech or quoted passage runs across a paragraph break, the CONTINUATION paragraph is not given a fresh dash but instead opens with a bare » with no matching « anywhere since the speech began — verified in context: '— Lo primero en que reparáis...' runs on, then '»En lo de citar...' and '»En lo que toca...' open the next two paragraphs, with zero « between them. A short, self-contained quotation instead gets an ordinary balanced pair on one paragraph ('«Apenas había el rubicundo…Montiel».'). This explains the measured 57 « vs 290 » imbalance across the whole 2.2MB work: most » are continuation markers, not closing quotes.
rules.action: When fired, treat a »-initial paragraph as continuing the nearest preceding unclosed speech/quotation rather than starting or ending a new one; do not pair it against the next available « (there may be none for a long stretch).

rules.name: Quotation-mark style is a property of the transcription, not of the declared language

rules.name: Gutenberg plaintext verse carries no per-line editorial numbering
rules.scope: Re-grounds and narrows seed S3 by source type: Gutenberg-plaintext-sourced verse (this territory) vs. Wikisource-apparatus verse (S3's original evidence base, Martial/Homer/Pindar, outside this territory and not re-checked by me).
rules.statement: S3 is implemented here exactly as originally stated (a trailing number is editorial lineation when essentially all such numbers are multiples of 5, k-of-k under a p=1/5 null giving 0.2^k), so the SAME detector could still fire on a Wikisource-style text. Run on three Gutenberg-plaintext verse ORIGINALS instead (Aeneid, Dante, Faust — 30,430 combined non-blank body lines), it finds ZERO trailing-number lines in any of them. S3's signature simply does not occur in this pipeline's source material; the rule's scope narrows to scholarly-apparatus transcriptions (Wikisource and similar), not verse in general, purely from an honest negative count.
rules.action: Do not look for or attempt to parse a per-line numbering apparatus in a Gutenberg-plaintext verse file; if editorial line numbers are needed, count lines directly instead of trusting/parsing a margin apparatus that isn't there.

rules.name: Tag-boundary space insertion (re-grounds S10)
rules.scope: zh.wikisource.org plain-text extractions produced by this corpus's HTML-to-text step, any work. Does not apply to the wikitext or the rendered HTML themselves, which carry no such whitespace; a rare true exception exists inside hand-typed template-parameter values (e.g. a header field's section-title text), which is not running prose.
rules.statement: The extraction inserts one ASCII space at (effectively) every HTML tag boundary crossed while flattening to text -- block (p/h2/div) and inline (span/a) alike -- regardless of whether the source HTML had whitespace there. Symptoms: every non-blank rendered line both starts and ends with a space; an empty block becomes a lone-space line; every {{專|}}/{{書|}}/link span gets a leading AND trailing space even mid-sentence.
rules.port: pending — a reference detector held under falsification; to be expressed as an organ primitive + table before the organ runs it
rules.narrowedScope: The underlying phenomenon (naive tag-boundary flattening inserts a space at every rendered line's start AND end) is real and reproduces on fresh content via an independent generic flattener -- lineEdgeFraction and loneSpaceBlankLines cleanly separate every original (exactly 0/0 across 21 fresh + several proposer files) from every flattened/extracted text (0.43-0.90) with zero overlap. But the rule's ACTUAL firing test (interiorCJKFlankedSpaces > 0, deliberately chosen over a fraction threshold per the detector's own comment) is refuted: it misfires on 4 of 21 genuine fresh originals I tested (19%), including the two files the rule already claimed to have checked. A corrected detector should fire on lineEdgeFraction/loneSpaceBlankLines, not on bare interior-space presence.
rules.counterexample: originals/bencao-caozhiyi.wikitext.txt, an UNMODIFIED original wikitext file the rule's own source comment names as already checked ('checked: shiji-juan001, bencao-caozhiyi, etc'): '《神農本草經》一百六十二種（梁陶弘景注） 《名醫別錄》一百三十一種（陶弘景注...）' -- real text has a bare ASCII space between '）' and '《' as an authorial bibliography-list separator, repeated 223 times (55% of all spaces in the file). Also originals/shiji-juan001.wikitext.txt: '| section  = 卷一 五帝本紀第一' -- a genuine juan-number/title heading separator, likewise present in shiji-juan002 and in shiji-juan001.html.

rules.name: Simplified-script UI chrome embedded in Traditional-script content (re-grounds S4)
rules.scope: Any zh.wikisource.org page whose content script is Traditional (true of every work in this territory). Does not fire on -{zh-hans:...;zh-hant:...}- LanguageConverter blocks (masked before scanning) or on documents that are genuinely majority-Simplified.

'Any rendered page with >=1 heading' must be read strictly as a wikitext section heading, not just substantial page content; confirmed on two independent targets, including the proposal's own suggested example.

rules.name: 索隱述贊 eulogy + 評論 heading are genuine source content, two distinct 'other hands' (re-grounds the core Shiji clause of S14)
rules.scope: 史記/卷NNN (plain edition) chapters with a biography/judgement structure. Absent from the opening annals chapter (五帝本紀, 卷001); 太史公曰 (but not 索隱述贊) also appears in the author's own postface (卷130) since Sima Qian there quotes his father and himself.
rules.statement: 史記/卷007's own fresh wikitext contains a real '==評論==' heading (Wikisource-editorial, marking Sima Qian's own 太史公曰 authorial-judgement voice) and a bracketed '【索隱述贊】' marker (introducing Tang scholar Sima Zhen's verse eulogy, a second, later hand). Both are present before any rendering or extraction -- genuine content, not conversion noise -- but they are two DIFFERENT voices, not one phenomenon as the seed's wording loosely groups them.
rules.port: pending — a reference detector held under falsification; to be expressed as an organ primitive + table before the organ runs it
rules.narrowedScope: The core claim -- that these two markers, where present, are genuine unmodified wikitext content rather than conversion artifacts -- holds (confirmed again on fresh 卷002's clean absence and fresh evidence on 卷130). But the scope's framing of 卷001 as essentially the sole annals-chapter exception is too narrow: 卷002 (also an early, legendary-dynasty annals chapter) is equally absent, so the real boundary is closer to 'early legendary-dynasty 本紀 chapters generally lack a closing judgment,' not 'only 卷001 lacks it.' Separately, the detector file's own source comment misstates 卷130's measured 太史公曰 count as 0 when the actual value (confirmed by its own code) is 4 -- a documentation defect distinct from, but adjacent to, the scope error.

rules.name: Vertical-text presentation-form colon before quoted commentary speech
rules.scope: Commentary quotations in this territory's annotated editions (measured on Yang Liang's Xunzi commentary); not yet checked against narrative (non-commentary) direct speech, which may use ordinary punctuation.
rules.statement: Commentary text introduces direct quotation with U+FE30 'PRESENTATION FORM FOR VERTICAL TWO DOT LEADER' (︰) rather than the ordinary horizontal fullwidth colon U+FF1A (：). Unicode's own character name records the vertical-text heritage: this is the glyph a vertical-column edition uses where a horizontal edition would use '：'. Its presence is a mechanical trace of a vertical-original edition's punctuation, readable without any page image.

rules.name: Duplicate-block-by-shift (overlapping/aliased subpage concatenation)
rules.scope: Any concatenated multi-subpage extraction in any script/language. Requires non-trivial (>=12 char) lines and a genuinely contiguous duplicated block of >=20 lines recurring at ONE fixed lag; will not catch duplication limited to short refrains, or duplicated content that was re-edited between the two fetches (no longer byte-identical).
rules.statement: If a text contains a contiguous run of >=20 non-trivial lines that recur verbatim at one fixed, nonzero line-offset, with that offset collecting >=20x more duplicate-line pairs than a random-offset null predicts, the text was very likely assembled by concatenating two overlapping or alias-duplicate page fetches.
rules.port: pending — a reference detector held under falsification; to be expressed as an organ primitive + table before the organ runs it
rules.narrowedScope: The >=20-contiguous-line requirement is doing essentially all the discriminating work; the >=20x-enrichment-over-a-random-lag-null statistic, which the rule's own write-up foregrounds as the key evidence, is NOT itself selective. All three independent near-miss/control texts tried (Homer's Iliad and Odyssey -- genuine oral-formulaic verbatim repeats -- and Boethius's prose) exceed the 20x enrichment bar purely from ordinary incidental phrase recurrence (39x-177x), and are saved from firing only by their longest contiguous match falling at 1-3 lines, far under the 20-line floor. The rule as coded still correctly never fires on a near-miss, but a reader should not treat '20x over a chance null' as meaningfully rare in real prose/verse -- it isn't.

rules.name: Wikisource title-alias-chain risk (redirect / label-vs-target delimiter mismatch)
rules.scope: MediaWiki wikis generally for the redirect-magic-word half (table currently covers the language-independent #REDIRECT plus ar/ru/fr/de/el localized aliases -- untested on a wiki outside that table). The label/target-mismatch half only fires on a TOC that gives per-part links an explicit custom display label different from its slash-delimited target; it is a RISK flag from text alone (it does not itself query the live redirects table), confirmed as a REAL collision only by a separate API lookup. It also does NOT catch multi-work disambiguation pages that use a template (e.g. Cyrillic {{Неоднозначность}}) rather than the #REDIRECT keyword -- verified as a real, current gap below.
rules.statement: A work root/TOC page that is itself a redirect, or whose per-part links show a target using one delimiter before a trailing number and a display label using a different delimiter before the same number, is at risk of being double-fetched by any subpage-discovery step that is not strict about resolving to canonical titles before deduplicating.
rules.port: pending — a reference detector held under falsification; to be expressed as an organ primitive + table before the organ runs it
rules.narrowedScope: The target/label delimiter-mismatch half only examines links whose target ends in slash+ARABIC-DIGIT and whose label ends in space+the-SAME-digit (regex requires \d{1,3} on both sides). Every other classical per-book TOC convention I found on original wikisource pages -- roman numerals (Martial, la.wikisource: 'Liber I'/'Liber I', matched) and Greek letters (Iliad, el.wikisource: Α/Β/Γ..., not digits at all) -- is structurally invisible to this regex regardless of whether a mismatch exists, not merely absent of one. rules.name: Stub-vs-reference (severe under-fetch of a multi-part work)
rules.scope: Primary path requires an independent character count freshly re-measured from the SAME declared source (strongest) or a same-work cross-edition proxy (weaker, as used for the French case here). The ratio<0.5 threshold is conservative, justified by measurement: no single top-level division of either multi-part classic surveyed here reaches half the total, so it would not misfire on a fetch that legitimately grabbed exactly one whole natural division. A work with only 2 roughly-equal top-level divisions could legitimately sit near the 0.5 boundary. The fallback (no reference available) is weak and text-intrinsic; it did NOT catch the French stub in testing precisely because that stub happens to end mid-dialogue, not mid-footnote-run -- illustrating why the primary, grounded path should always be preferred when obtainable.
rules.statement: A text that is a small fraction (<50%) of a fresh, independent measurement of the same declared source (or an appropriate cross-edition proxy) was very likely produced by a fetch loop that stopped partway through a multi-part/multi-subpage work, not by a legitimately narrow fetch scope.
rules.port: pending — a reference detector held under falsification; to be expressed as an organ primitive + table before the organ runs it
rules.narrowedScope: The primary (grounded, reference-recount) path held cleanly on both texts tested. The fallback (text-intrinsic, no-reference) path -- which the rule's own comments already call 'weak... not proof' -- produces a real, concrete false positive whenever a text's last real section happens to be legitimately footnote-dense: Brillat-Savarin's live_priors extraction ends '↑ Henrion de Pansey .' after 11 consecutive footnote-backlink lines with no closing marker, so the fallback alone reports fired=true ('looks like a stopped-mid-fetch stub'), while the primary path (a fresh reference) shows the SAME text is 165% of an independent re-measurement -- i.e. not remotely a stub. This is the rule's own disclosed weakness, now demonstrated with real bytes rather than only asserted.
rules.counterexample: live_priors brillat-savarin-physiologie-du-gout.txt, last non-blank line: '↑ Henrion de Pansey .' (11th consecutive footnote-backlink line) -- fallback path fires 'stub', but ctx.referenceChars-grounded primary path gives ratio=1.65 (complete, not a stub).

rules.name: Dropped inline honorific template (Arabic Hadith texts)
rules.scope: ar.wikisource Hadith/religious texts using the {{صل}} template convention specifically (confirmed on Bukhari and Fihrist, both showing near-total drop; a THIRD work from the same collection, Ibn al-Haytham's Book of Optics, shows the honorific SURVIVING at a 22% rate, proving the extraction pipeline's behavior is inconsistent even within one live_priors collection, not that the rule is wrong). Does not generalize without separate verification to other honorific/devotional templates (e.g. {{رضي}} for companions) or to non-Arabic religious texts.
rules.statement: In an Arabic religious/legal text where the Prophet's name/title is mentioned at least 5 times, if fewer than 5% of those mentions carry an honorific mark (the ﷺ ligature or its spelled-out phrase), the source's inline honorific template was dropped by the extraction pipeline for the great majority of its occurrences.
rules.port: pending — a reference detector held under falsification; to be expressed as an organ primitive + table before the organ runs it
rules.narrowedScope: The core claim generalizes cleanly to a second, independent Hadith collection (Sahih Muslim) with even tighter grounding than the original (same page for both the wikitext template-count and the rendered-text survival count). But the exact-substring NAME_MENTIONS matcher (['النبي','رسول الله']) is blind to fully-diacritized (tashkil) Arabic: Quran sura al-Ahzab literally opens 'يَا أَيُّهَا النَّبِيُّ' (O Prophet...) and contains 16 real 'النبي' mentions once combining marks are stripped, yet the matcher counts 0 because the vowel marks sit between the letters. On this near-miss the wrong count coincidentally still lands on the correct verdict (not enough signal -> no-fire, and the Quran genuinely never used {{صل}}), but the same blindness would silently mask a real dropped-honorific case on any fully-vocalized Hadith edition, reporting 'not enough signal' instead of either a correct pass or a correct flag.
rules.counterexample: ar.wikisource Quran, sura al-Ahzab v.1: 'يَا أَيُّهَا النَّبِيُّ اتَّقِ اللَّهَ' -- literal substring 'النبي' count = 0; diacritic-stripped count = 16.

rules.scope: Wikisource-platform-wide (ProofreadPage extension), confirmed on 3 languages (ru, fr, de) and 2 distinct transclusion idioms (a single <pages from=X to=Y/> range tag; a sequence of per-printed-page {{SeitePR|...}} calls). Does not itself determine whether a given work uses this convention or plain inline wikitext -- that has to be checked per page, which is what this detector does. The gap-based statistic (for >=2 markers) is robust to genuine apparatus text surrounding the transcluded run; the whole-document fallback (for exactly 1 marker) sufficed for both single-tag cases found here.
rules.statement: If a Wikisource page's wikitext contains 2+ page-transclusion markers ({{SeitePR|...}} or <pages .../>) with no more than ~20 characters of real content between any consecutive pair, or exactly one <pages .../> tag and fewer than 300 characters of prose remaining once it and the leading metadata template are stripped, the page's actual text is not present in its own wikitext -- fetching prop=wikitext here yields none of the work's real content.
rules.port: pending — a reference detector held under falsification; to be expressed as an organ primitive + table before the organ runs it

rules.name: Unexpanded template-parameter placeholder leak
rules.scope: General across any MediaWiki-sourced text: literal '{{{PARAM}}}' syntax can never be genuine prose in any language. rules.statement: Literal triple-brace MediaWiki parameter syntax (e.g. {{{WIKIDATA}}}) appearing in extracted text always indicates an unexpanded template-parameter reference; check the ORIGINAL's own rendered HTML before assuming the extractor introduced it, because it can already be present there.

rules.name: {{Kapitaelchen}} predicts small-caps rendering (CV fact from a byte signature)
rules.scope: de.wikisource specifically (confirmed template name); other wikis may use a differently-named small-caps template (not yet catalogued here) or CSS-class-based markup instead of a template, which this detector would miss.
rules.statement: A {{Kapitaelchen|NAME}} (or {{Kapitälchen|NAME}}) template call in de.wikisource wikitext predicts that NAME is rendered in small capital letters on the printed/scanned page -- a purely visual distinction a CV/OCR look would show and plain-text extraction cannot represent -- without needing to render or look at the page at all.
rules.port: pending — a reference detector held under falsification; to be expressed as an organ primitive + table before the organ runs it
rules.narrowedScope: The mechanical rendering claim (this template's argument is rendered font-variant:small-caps) held on a second, fully independent de.wikisource work (RE:Aulon 1, a classical-geography encyclopedia entry, nothing to do with Frege). But the rule's framing -- 'predicts a cited scholar's NAME' -- is narrower than the template's real use: the one argument found in this fresh instance is 'III' (a volume-number citation inside 'CIA III 61'), not a person's name. The same snippet also contains {{SperrSchrift|Bursian}} -- a sibling German typographic-emphasis convention (letter-spacing/'Sperrdruck', the traditional way German scholarship emphasizes a cited name, arguably MORE common than small-caps for this purpose) applied to an actual scholar's surname, structurally invisible to this detector because it only looks for Kapitaelchen/Kapitälchen.

rules.name: Every-5-lines verse numbering (re-grounds S3 with the source mechanism)
rules.scope: Verse works on la.wikisource using the {{r|{{safesubst:#invoke:Romanus|Arabic|BOOK}}.N|N}} citation template inside <poem> blocks (confirmed for Martial); does not itself confirm the SAME template is used for Homer/Pindar on Greek Wikisource (named in the seed) -- those would need their own wikitext check.
rules.statement: If a work's trailing line-end integers are multiples of 5 far more often than an independent p=1/5 null would predict (binomial-tail p<1e-6, with >=20 samples), the work almost certainly carries an explicit every-5-lines verse-numbering convention in its source, not an extraction coincidence.
rules.port: pending — a reference detector held under falsification; to be expressed as an organ primitive + table before the organ runs it
rules.narrowedScope: The underlying statistical claim generalizes robustly -- confirmed on Homer via a template mechanism ({{fr|N}}) that is CONFIRMED DIFFERENT from Martial's ({{r|{{safesubst:#invoke:Romanus|...}}}}), verified directly in el.wikisource's own Page:-namespace source. But the detector needs RENDERED/expanded text, not raw wikitext, to see the pattern at all: Martial's raw wikitext embeds the number inside the template call itself ('...sentienti,{{r|...|5}}\nRari...'), so the digit never sits bare immediately before a newline, and the detector correctly reports 'too few samples' on a page where the convention is unquestionably present. Separately, a real but differently-shaped every-line (not every-5th) numbering convention exists on a different la.wikisource Boethius edition (Migne, numbers precede rather than follow each verse) that this trailing-number regex cannot see -- a distinct convention from what this rule targets, not a counterexample to its actual claim, but it means 'expect fire' was not automatically transferable to that edition as the held-out suggestion assumed.

rules.name: The GRETIL sigla bracket, not the newline, is the true unit boundary
rules.scope: GRETIL corpustei plaintext transformations whose citation uses an alphabetic-prefix + underscore + number pattern bracketed by 1-2 daNDa/pipe marks on at least the opening side (ps_/jaim_/kvs_/mmk_/bhn_/ys_/BSS_/KSak_-style). Does NOT cover Nyāyasūtra's bare 'N.N.N:' colon convention or Sāṃkhyakārikā's bracket-free 'SK_N' convention -- found and confirmed by running this detector against both (see heldOut).
rules.statement: A GRETIL work's true unit count equals the number of sigla-bracket matches, not the physical line count -- newlines are sometimes entirely absent (Pāṇini: 3951 sigla on effectively 1 real body line) yet the sigla stream survives intact and is trivially re-segmentable.
rules.port: pending — a reference detector held under falsification; to be expressed as an organ primitive + table before the organ runs it
rules.narrowedScope: Recovers an accurate unit count only when the citation's pipe/slash sits immediately (whitespace-only gap) before the alphabetic prefix in every instance. A same-family colon-terminated mula+bhasya convention that happens to sit near an unrelated neighboring daNDa does not cleanly return zero (as the two already-known excluded conventions do) -- it can return a small, confidently-labeled, badly wrong count instead.
rules.counterexample: nyayasutra-comm-plaintext.txt: real citation form is ' nys_1,1.1: pramāṇaprameya...niḥśreyasādhigamaḥ ||' (colon after the number, no pipe/slash before it). Detector reports totalSigla=10 (fired:true) when the true recoverable unit count is >=498 -- a >98% undercount, not a clean rejection.

rules.name: Bare <l> vs <lg>-wrapped <l> in the TEI predicts GRETIL's own flattening
rules.scope: GRETIL corpustei TEI source files (the cause is checked on the ORIGINAL markup, not on any plaintext extraction). Verified across all 8 TEI files fetched for this territory.
rules.statement: GRETIL's TEI-to-plaintext transform emits a newline after every </l> that sits inside an <lg> (lineGroup), but emits nothing between consecutive bare <l> elements with no <lg> parent -- so a work encoded as thousands of bare <l> (the prose-sutra convention) collapses onto one line, while a work whose verses are grouped in <lg> keeps one line per pāda.
rules.port: pending — a reference detector held under falsification; to be expressed as an organ primitive + table before the organ runs it
rules.narrowedScope:
Holds as an exact predictor of flattening only for works whose GRETIL TEI tags its sutra/pada units as at all. It is blind to (Nyayasutra) or actively wrong about (Kamasutra) works whose encoder instead used bare

for the same units, even though GRETIL's transform applies the identical silence-on-bare-tag behavior to

.
rules.counterexample: kamasutra-tei.xml: predictedFlattened=false (from 4 incidental lg-wrapped <l>), yet its true plaintext body packs an entire chapter's ~30 sutras into one ~20,000-character line -- a wrong affirmative prediction, not mere silence.

falsification.target: kanada-alt-tei.xml (new, alt edition of in-set work)
falsification.measured: bareL=369, lgWrappedL=0, predictedFlattened=true; matches the alt edition's actual plaintext (maxLineShareOfTotal=1.0) exactly

rules.name: Sigla case reveals whether it was typed as text or synthesized from an ID
rules.scope: GRETIL works whose sigla prefix is uniform in case within the work (single-register prose or verse works). Explicitly falsified on mixed-genre drama (see heldOut: Śakuntalā uses TWO deliberate casings for a different reason).
rules.statement: A sigla prefix typed as literal text by the TEI encoder gets lowercased by GRETIL's transform (PS_->ps_, Jaim_->jaim_, MMK_->mmk_...); a sigla synthesized from an @xml:id attribute is copied verbatim and keeps its authored case (Brahmagupta's BSS_ stays uppercase) because it never passes through whatever normalization pass lowercases literal text.

rules.name: Daṇḍa glyphs: citation-only in prose sūtra vs also-prosodic in verse
rules.scope: IAST GRETIL texts using '|'/'||' or '/'/'//' as their citation delimiter. An earlier version of this detector (naive lone-vs-paired counting) was WRONG for single-glyph-bracket works (Jaimini, Kaṇāda) and was rewritten after being caught by actually running it -- see evidence.
rules.statement: In a prose sūtra work the daNDa glyph exists ONLY as the citation bracket: essentially 100% of its occurrences sit inside a sigla match. In a metrical verse work the SAME glyph is also a live prosody mark: a large, non-trivial share of its occurrences sit in running verse text, unattached to any citation.
rules.port: pending — a reference detector held under falsification; to be expressed as an organ primitive + table before the organ runs it
rules.counterexample: Manusmrti and Raghuvamsha verses are formatted as two padas per physical line-pair with a plain NEWLINE as the only pada separator and the glyph reserved for the closing bracket only, e.g. 'vāgarthāv iva saṃpṛktau vāgarthapratipattaye \njagataḥ pitarau vande pārvatīparameśvarau // Ragh_1.1' -- textbook verse, zero mid-verse '/'. Conversely nyayasutra-comm's bhāṣya prose uses '/' throughout as ordinary sentence-final punctuation, e.g. 'pravṛttisāmarthyād arthavat pramāṇam/ ... arthas tu sukhaṃ sukhahetuś ca, duḥkhaṃ duḥkhahetuś ca/' -- prose, but reads as 99.8% 'unaccounted'.

falsification.measured: unaccountedShare=0.0009, classified 'prose sutra (no independent meter)' -- wrong

falsification.measured: unaccountedShare=0.0015, classified 'prose sutra (no independent meter)' -- wrong

falsification.measured: unaccountedShare=0.9983, classified 'verse karika (metrical pada structure)' -- wrong

falsification.measured: unaccountedShare=0, correct

falsification.target: aryabhatiya-plaintext.txt / bhagavatapurana-plaintext.txt (new, control, verse)
falsification.measured: unaccountedShare=0.34 / 0.22, correct

evidence.source: BUG CAUGHT BY RUNNING: first version flagged Jaimini/Kaṇāda (both prose) as 'verse' because they use a SINGLE '/' or '|' bracket (two lone marks per citation) rather than a doubled one; rewrote to measure share of the glyph's TOTAL occurrences consumed by citation brackets, regardless of doubling style

rules.name: ASCII word-class regex silently truncates IAST words at diacritics
rules.scope: Any IAST-transliterated text (all of GRETIL's output, both corpustei-TEI-plaintext and legacy-HTML pipelines). Re-grounds seed S1 specifically for Romanized-not-native-script Indic text.
rules.statement: Unlike Devanagari/Chinese/Arabic (where S1's ASCII classes return EMPTY), IAST is Latin-alphabet-based, so /[a-zA-Z]+/ does not fail visibly -- it returns a plausible-looking WRONG fragment. Any whitespace token containing an IAST diacritic (ā ī ū ṛ ṃ ḥ ṅ ñ ṭ ḍ ṇ ś ṣ etc.) gets split into 2+ separate regex matches at the diacritic, so first/last-word or syllable-count logic keyed on that regex silently returns a truncated non-word, never a signal to fall back.
rules.port: pending — a reference detector held under falsification; to be expressed as an organ primitive + table before the organ runs it

falsification.measured: splitShareOfDiacriticTokens between 0.73 and 0.89 in all 5, consistent with the original training set

falsification.target: synthetic ASCII-only control ('The quick brown fox... no diacritics at all')
falsification.expected: not-fire, per the rule's own disclosed falsification boundary
falsification.measured: tokensWithDiacritic=0, splitCount=0 -- confirms the boundary exactly

rules.name: Citation-number periods are not sentence ends
rules.scope: Any GRETIL plaintext using period-grouped numeric citations (chapter,pada.number). Re-grounds seed S15 for this territory.
rules.statement: GRETIL sigla numbers use '.' as a grouping separator (e.g. '1,1.1', '6,1.130'), immediately followed by a space then the closing bracket. A naive /\.\s/ sentence-splitter fires INSIDE the citation, not at the real unit boundary a few characters later -- and in these prose sūtra works essentially every period in the whole document is one of these false-trigger sites, because the convention has no other use for a period at all.
rules.port: pending — a reference detector held under falsification; to be expressed as an organ primitive + table before the organ runs it
rules.narrowedScope: The 'essentially every period is a false-trigger site' framing holds only for 2-part, single-embedded-period citations immediately followed by a closing bracket. It measurably weakens (still real, but ~47% not ~100%) for 3-part citations, and it misses the underlying problem entirely on any convention whose citation number is not bracket-terminated, even when a genuine naive-splitter hazard is present and arguably worse (mid-sentence rather than at a unit boundary).
rules.counterexample: Kamasutra: 1397 real period-space citation-internal break opportunities exist by direct count; the bracket-anchored detector reports 0.

falsification.target: kanada-alt-plaintext.txt (new, 2-part comma+period citation)
falsification.expected: essentially all periods are false-trigger sites
falsification.measured: 94.6% (369/390) -- matches original Kanada's pattern

falsification.target: bhagavatapurana-plaintext.txt (new, 3-part chapter.pada.verse citation, N=14208)
falsification.expected: essentially all periods, per the rule's STATEMENT
falsification.measured: only 47.2% (14581/30883) -- real and substantial, but far from 'essentially every period', because only the LAST of two embedded periods per citation sits next to the closing bracket

falsification.target: manusmrti / raghuvamsha (new, number-at-end-of-line, no trailing bracket)
falsification.measured: 0 false-break sites -- verified this is CORRECT, not a miss: the citation number sits directly before a bare newline with no intervening space+bracket, so a plain \.\s splitter genuinely has no trigger there

falsification.target: kamasutra-plaintext.txt (new, bare numeric citation embedded in running prose, no bracket at all)
falsification.measured: detector reports 0 false-break sites, but a direct count of real 'digit.digit + space + letter' sites (no bracket required) finds 1397, e.g. '...śāstre prakṛtatvāt. 1.1.3 tatsamayāvabodhakebhyaś...' -- a naive splitter would genuinely misfire there 1397 times

evidence.measured: falseBreakSites=3951, totalPeriods=3974, shareOfPeriodsThatAreCitationInternal=0.9942 (99.4% of all periods in the file)
falseBreakSites=2726, totalPeriods=2752, share=0.9906
falseBreakSites=448, totalPeriods=464, share=0.9655 -- same phenomenon even where the body IS properly lined, since the hazard is about a splitter using periods, not newlines

rules.name: Legacy-HTML transliteration legend table leaks into extracted text
rules.scope: GRETIL's legacy pre-TEI HTML tree (1_sanskr/**) converted to plain text. Not present in the corpustei/TEI pipeline (no such table exists there). New finding, not in the seed list (S18 candidate) -- and the one artifact in this territory clearly attributable to the FETCH/EXTRACTION step rather than to GRETIL itself.
rules.statement: GRETIL's legacy HTML editions open with a real HTML <table> mapping an English description ('vocalic r', 'retroflex t'...) to its IAST character -- a human-facing font/encoding legend, not text of the work. A naive HTML-to-text conversion that strips tags but keeps cell text turns this into dozens of consecutive short 'label / lone-diacritic-letter' lines sitting between the provenance note and the first real verse. Detection is structural (a run of short ASCII-description + non-ASCII-character lines), never a hardcoded list of the ~40 actual legend labels.
rules.port: pending — a reference detector held under falsification; to be expressed as an organ primitive + table before the organ runs it

falsification.target: mbh02-legacy.htm / mbh06-legacy.htm, fed as completely raw .htm bytes
falsification.measured: longestLegendShapedRun=0 -- but the SAME null result reproduces on the rule's own original grounding file (bhagavadgita.htm) under the identical raw-bytes test, showing the detector's real input contract is HTML-to-text-CONVERTED plain text, not raw markup; the rule's true positive evidence lives in a live_priors post-conversion copy (35-line run), not the raw file

falsification.target: mbh02-legacy.htm / mbh06-legacy.htm, fed through a genuinely naive tag-stripper (delete tags, keep the source's own line breaks, no synthetic newlines added)
falsification.expected: fire, ~35-40 line run, per the rule's explicit held-out suggestion
falsification.measured: both reproduce a 35-consecutive-line run, an exact match to bhagavadgita.htm's own 35-line run under the same conversion

falsification.target: manusmrti / raghuvamsha / bhagavatapurana plaintext (new, corpustei pipeline, never HTML)
falsification.measured: longestLegendShapedRun=0 in all three, correct

evidence.measured: longestLegendShapedRun=0, fired=false -- confirms the artifact does NOT exist in the source's own on-screen form, only after tag-stripping

rules.name: HTML-to-text join inserts a space at inline-tag boundaries that have none in the source
rules.scope:
Any el.wikisource plain-text extraction produced by walking rendered HTML. Bracket sub-check fires only when the bracket's interior contains a NESTED inline element (a self-link span, as in Republic's Stephanus refs); plain-text-only brackets (Sophist's literal '[ἑταίρων]', no nested tag) do not trigger it. Trailing-space sub-check fires only on /
-structured verse; prose paragraphs (Hippocrates) do not trigger it.
rules.statement:
Where the rendered HTML has zero whitespace between a bracket character and an inline tag it wraps, the plain-text extraction inserts one anyway; and every non-final line of a
-delimited verse block gets one synthetic trailing space before its newline.
rules.port: pending — a reference detector held under falsification; to be expressed as an organ primitive + table before the organ runs it
rules.narrowedScope:
The tag-boundary space-injection mechanism is real and broader than stated: it also fires from one-utterance-per-line PROSE rendering (a stray-newline-adjacent

boundary), not only
-in- verse. But the specific sub-claim 'prose paragraphs do not trigger the trailing-space sub-check' is false in general -- it depends on whether the wikitext is typed one utterance per line (Parmenides: fires) or in flowing multi-sentence paragraphs (Hippocrates-style: does not).

Παρμενίδης wikitext contains zero literal
tags and is plain narrated PROSE (see flattened/el-parmenides.txt), yet 97.2% of its mid-block lines carry the synthetic trailing space the rule's own text claims is specific to '/

rules.name: <word> marks an editorial conjecture, and this pipeline silently deletes the mark

rules.port: pending — a reference detector held under falsification; to be expressed as an organ primitive + table before the organ runs it
