rules.name: Not every Platonic dialogue uses recurring speaker-abbreviation labels
rules.scope: Plato's dialogues on el.wikisource. A direct, source-grounded scope-limiter for seed S11.
rules.statement: Some dialogues (Sophist, and by seed S11's own numbers Theaetetus/Statesman/Parmenides) are staged as pure drama with a recurring all-caps speaker lead ending in a period at the start of nearly every turn; the Republic instead is written as Socrates' first-person NARRATED report, using reporting verbs ('ἔφη', 'ἦν δ' ἐγώ') and carrying NO recurring speaker-label lead at all -- a rule built only from dramatic-dialogue evidence over-generalizes.
rules.port: pending — a reference detector held under falsification; to be expressed as an organ primitive + table before the organ runs it
rules.narrowedScope: The recurring-all-caps-speaker-lead mechanism correctly separates Theaetetus/Sophist from Republic, but Parmenides -- named explicitly by the rule as an expected dramatic case -- is entirely narrated on this el.wikisource transcription. Phaedo also complicates the stated binary: its 'dramatic' classification rests on a thin frame (13/16 occurrences of only the two frame-speakers, Phaedo and Echecrates) wrapped around a heavily narrated inner account (389 reporting-verb hits, far more than Theaetetus's 17), so the detector is really measuring how THIS PARTICULAR TRANSCRIPTION chose to typeset the dialogue, not a fixed literary property of the work itself.
rules.counterexample: flattened/el-parmenides.txt opens: 'Κέφαλος: ἐπειδὴ Ἀθήναζε οἴκοθεν ἐκ Κλαζομενῶν ἀφικόμεθα, κατ᾽ ἀγορὰν ἐνετύχομεν Ἀδειμάντῳ τε καὶ Γλαύκωνι: καί μου λαβόμενος τῆς χειρὸς ὁ Ἀδείμαντος, Χαῖρ᾽, ἔφη, ὦ Κέφαλε...' -- narrated throughout via reporting verbs ('ἔφη') with mixed-case names (not ALL-CAPS sigla), in exactly the style the rule attributes only to Republic.

rules.name: Standalone Eddukvæði verse is dd-per-line, not hard-wrapped (re-grounds S2)
rules.scope: heimskringla.no's STANDALONE Eddukvæði poems only (6/6 measured). Does NOT extend to verse quoted inline within prose narration, even on heimskringla.no's own Gylfaginning page (0 '::' lines there) -- the split tracks GENRE (standalone edition vs. prose-embedded citation), not site.
rules.statement: Every metrical half-line of a standalone Eddukvæði poem is marked with a MediaWiki definition-indent '::' (one <dd> per line); stanza numbers get their own '::N.' line; a blank-spacer line ':: ' separates stanzas. This is deliberate lineation, not hard-wrap-and-reflow: replaying seed S2's own wrap-detection formula on the extracted body lines of 6 poems gives brokenFrac 2.4%-22.2% (all far under S2's 50% 'wrapped' cutoff), with line-length coefficient-of-variation 0.18-0.26 (real wrapped prose clusters tightly near its wrap width; this does not). MediaWiki-sourced PROSE paragraphs, by contrast, are stored as one very long unwrapped line each (measured mean 337 chars, up to 1641, in Gylfaginning) -- S2's antecedent (multiple interior lines to test) does not even arise for wiki-sourced prose, only for deliberately-lineated verse.
rules.port: pending — a reference detector held under falsification; to be expressed as an organ primitive + table before the organ runs it
rules.counterexample: heim-voluspa-hauksbok.wikitext.txt and heim-voluspo-propvariant.wikitext.txt are both standalone Eddukvæði-genre Völuspá editions hosted on heimskringla.no -- the exact category the rule claims to cover -- with the dd-per-line convention plainly present (504 and 597 lines beginning with '::'). Both report fired:false because their stanza numbers are typeset bold ("::'''66.'''") rather than plain ("::66."), which the detector's stanzaNumberLines test (/^:+\d+\.$/) does not match.

rules.name:
'
  ' forces a paragraph/speaker break invisible to blank-line splitting
rules.scope: Snorra Edda prose narration (Gylfaginning, Skáldskaparmál, Háttatal) on EITHER site -- confirmed byte-identical between heimskringla.no's and is.wikisource's copies of Gylfaginning.
rules.statement:
MediaWiki collapses a single '\n' inside a paragraph to a space; Snorra Edda's transcription instead forces many internal breaks with a literal '
  ' (line break + 2 non-breaking spaces, mimicking a printed paragraph's indent) with NO blank line, so the break is invisible to any blank-line-based paragraph splitter. Measured marker counts: Gylfaginning 185 (identical on both sites' copies), Skáldskaparmál 112, Háttatal 80. A closed table of named interlocutors (Hárr/Jafnhárr/Þriði/Gangleri/Bragi/Ægir/...) immediately follows the marker in a genre-dependent subset (39/185 in Gylfaginning, 3/112 in Skáldskaparmál, 0/80 in Háttatal's anonymous catechism register); most of the remainder continue with the anaphoric pronoun 'Þá' ('then') rather than a name -- a stated, deliberate coverage gap of the closed table, not evidence the marker itself is 'merely' generic.

rules.name: -only line breaks get doubled into blank-separated paragraphs on extraction
rules.scope:
Any live_priors-style flattening of a passage whose ORIGINAL used a single literal '
' as its only line-break mechanism (a
-wrapped verse citation, or a plain
-separated name list) in this corpus. Confirmed on 2 verse citations + 1 name list, all within Snorra Edda; does NOT occur where the source instead used '::'/
(Eddukvæði proper).
rules.statement:
Where Snorri's prose quotes Eddic verse (wikitext:
+ one
per line, zero blank lines) or lists names (wikitext: bare
-per-name, zero blank lines), the live_priors flattened extraction (snorra-edda.txt) turns every single '
' into a paragraph break, inserting a blank line after each one -- producing long, perfectly-alternating text/blank/text/blank runs that are exponentially unlikely under the file's own blank-line rate. The SAME pipeline handles the OTHER Old Norse verse convention in this corpus ('::'/
, see eddic-dd-per-line-verse.mjs) correctly, with blanks only at genuine stanza gaps -- this is a pipeline inconsistency specific to bare '
' breaks, not a general defect.
rules.port: pending — a reference detector held under falsification; to be expressed as an organ primitive + table before the organ runs it
rules.narrowedScope:
The alternating-run signal is reliable evidence of THIS specific live_priors
->paragraph-break bug only when used the way the rule's own text uses it: paired with a direct diff against the matching passage's original wikitext (which shows zero interior blank lines at that exact spot). Read in isolation, 'fired:true' on an arbitrary file is not diagnostic of this specific pipeline defect -- it is a generic 'looks like a one-entry-per-paragraph list' signature that also fires on unrelated, non-buggy natural text, and it sits uncomfortably close to its own significance threshold even on a genuine non-artifactual alternation already present inside this corpus's own originals.
rules.counterexample:
live_priors/11-multi-language/translations-en/bellows-1923-the-poetic-edda.txt: an ordinary Gutenberg-style index ('Vāl′-i, a god, 15, 82, 198...' / blank / next glossary entry / blank / ...) trips the identical detector at corrected p=4.6e-25 -- as strong a signal as the confirmed snorra-edda.txt bug -- despite having no '
', no live_priors involvement, and no connection to Old Norse at all.

rules.name: eoreader7's [a-z]+ word regex fails on Old Norse's extended-Latin letters (extends S1)
rules.scope: Any Old Norse text (or similarly Latin-extended orthography) run through eoreader7's native/the-fold/medium.js first/last-word capture (lines 205 & 210: body.toLowerCase().replace(/[’']/g,'').match(/[a-z]+/)). Confirmed on both verse (Eddukvæði) and prose (Gylfaginning); confirmed NOT to fire on plain Modern English.
rules.statement: Old Norse routinely uses þ, ð, æ, ö and the acutes á/é/í/ó/ú/ý as ORDINARY alphabetic letters, not optional diacritics -- none of which match eoreader7's ASCII-only [a-z]+. Replaying that exact regex against true words from the fetched ORIGINAL wikitext mismatches (truncates or empties) 46.8% of Völuspá's words, 42.6% of Hávamál's, and 48.3% of Gylfaginning's prose -- comparable to seed S1's 98-100% failure rate on non-Latin scripts, but on a script S1's original survey (Chinese/Arabic/Greek/Devanagari/Russian) did not cover. The fire threshold (>8.3%) is 5x a MEASURED Modern-English control baseline (1.66%, 65/3927 words, from a Gutenberg-quality translation with its own residual typographic noise), not an assumed number. This WIDENS S1's scope from 'non-Latin scripts' to 'any Latin-extended orthography using letters outside a-z as ordinary letters.'

rules.name: Speaker-label line geometry (inline vs standalone) is per-edition, not per-period/language
rules.scope: Play-text speaker cues shaped "Label." at line-start, any language using Latin or Greek capitals; not prose narrative (rule-11) and not the Ancient-Greek abbreviation system itself (rule-04).
rules.statement: A work's recurring speaker label is set in one of two mutually exclusive geometries — INLINE (label and speech share one physical line) or STANDALONE (label alone on its own line, speech starts the next line) — and a single witness is overwhelmingly, not just mostly, one or the other. The choice tracks the EDITION, not the period or the language: the 1623 First Folio and a 19th-century (Dyce) edited Marlowe text share the OLD inline convention; a modern Gutenberg Shakespeare resetting and native German drama printing (Goethe) share the NEW standalone convention.
rules.port: pending — a reference detector held under falsification; to be expressed as an organ primitive + table before the organ runs it
rules.narrowedScope: Holds cleanly -- binary geometry, lopsided at p<1e-30, tracking the EDITION not language/period -- whenever the speaker cue is a bare 'Label.' with no surrounding transcription markup and no internal period. Does not extend to (silently reports zero qualifying labels rather than measuring) editions that wrap the cue in Gutenberg's leading/trailing underscore-italics convention, or that abbreviate a label with an internal period between tokens ('K. Edw.', 'Y. Mor.') -- both real, common Gutenberg drama-e-text conventions.
rules.counterexample: pg20288 (Marlowe, Edward II, Queipo transcription), raw bytes: 0 qualifying labels, reason 'no recurring ALL-CAPS/Titlecase label found'. Body reads '_Y. Mor._ Madam, farewell.' A diagnostic copy with every underscore stripped fires perfectly: 899/899 (100%) inline, log2p=-654 -- the true geometry was measurable all along, just hidden by markup the regex doesn't parse through.

rules.name: This Greek digitization collapses ano teleia/question-mark to plain ASCII semicolon
rules.scope: Modern digitizations of polytonic Ancient Greek (Wikisource, and expected on most plain-text OCT transcriptions); will differ on sources that keep the traditional glyphs.
rules.statement: Ancient Greek's own four-mark stop system (period, comma, ano teleia U+0387, and a semicolon-shaped question mark) is measurably collapsed in this digitization to three working marks: period, comma, and ASCII ';' doing question-mark duty. Proper U+0387/U+037E are effectively unused. A reader that assumes ';' means a weak pause (as in English) will read every Greek question in this corpus as a statement.
rules.port: pending — a reference detector held under falsification; to be expressed as an organ primitive + table before the organ runs it
rules.counterexample: Perseus/PerseusDL's independent canonical-greekLit TEI-XML edition of Plato's Apology (confirmed correctly identified: title 'Ἀπολογία Σωκράτους', author Plato, scanned at St. Olaf 1992, released 1996 -- a totally different institution/decade/pipeline than Greek Wikisource) shows the identical 'collapse': anoTeleia=0, greekQuestionMark=0, asciiSemicolon=82 -- directly contradicting the rule's stated scope 'Will differ on a source that deliberately keeps the traditional glyphs.' Verified this is structural, not coincidental: U+037E GREEK QUESTION MARK has a canonical Unicode decomposition to U+003B SEMICOLON (confirmed against Python's bundled Unicode Character Database v16.0.0 -- both NFC and NFD normalization of U+037E yield plain ';'), so the distinction is effectively unobservable in any text that has passed through ordinary Unicode normalization; it is not a deliberate, 'keepable' editorial choice the way the rule's scope implies.

A pipeline that treats prop=wikitext as "the source" — one of the two methods this very task brief suggests trying — gets almost nothing for this entire class of source; prop=text (server-side resolved) or walking the sub-pages is required.
rules.port: pending — a reference detector held under falsification; to be expressed as an organ primitive + table before the organ runs it
rules.counterexample: Three independently-fetched, genuinely thin Wikisource 'you fetched a stub, not the content' pages -- Republic's book-index/TOC page (546 real letters), the Comedy of Errors #REDIRECT (96 letters), and the facsimile-edition {{header}}+{{AuxTOC}} act-index page it redirects to (788 letters) -- all fail to fire because none carry the exact `<pages index=... from=... to=.../>` tag the regex requires, even though the detector already computes `letterCountOutsideTag` as a byproduct without using it as the firing condition.

rules.name: Scan-page-boundary paragraph seams are detectable in plain text, and mostly absent here
rules.scope: Any plain-text extraction of a ProofreadPage-transcluded work, any language; expected to almost never fire on a well-proofread Wikisource text and TO fire on a rougher transcription or a pipeline that reflowed paragraphs at fixed intervals.
rules.statement: The real per-page wikitext uses a '{{nop}}' template to suppress a spurious paragraph break when a sentence continues across a scan-page boundary. rules.name: Recurring multi-word role labels with zero abbreviated variant anywhere signal transcriber expansion
rules.scope: Gutenberg drama e-texts of this vintage/house style where a transcriber's note may or may not survive in the copy being read.
rules.statement: When every recurring multi-word ALL-CAPS role label in a text (e.g. SECOND SCHOLAR) has NO abbreviated variant of itself anywhere in the same text, and no explanatory note survives, that is the signature of transcriber-driven name expansion over a print edition that actually abbreviated — exactly what Gutenberg #779's own (elsewhere-dropped) production note says happened here. A positive result is a warning to re-fetch the source's own production notes, not proof by itself.
rules.port: pending — a reference detector held under falsification; to be expressed as an organ primitive + table before the organ runs it
rules.narrowedScope: The positive warning is sound and generalizes further than claimed (confirmed via an independent Folio cross-check on a target originally guessed to be a near miss). A NEGATIVE (not-fired) result should not be trusted as clean, because: (a) the label-finder has no speaker-cue-usage check, so scene headings ('SCENE II.') and running-head fragments ('OF DR.') get counted as if they were recurring speaker labels whenever a multi-scene play repeats a heading text >=3 times; (b) the abbreviation safety net tries only ONE shared truncation length across every word of a label, so it can never find a real, asymmetric abbreviation.
rules.counterexample: Unmodified original pg779 contains 'SEC. SCHOL.' in plain text (in the transcriber's own note, quoting the discarded form); `abbreviationVariantsExist('SECOND SCHOLAR', text)` still returns false for every truncation length 2 through 6, because no single shared length reproduces the real 3-letter+5-letter split -- confirmed with a controlled construction that rewords only the note's trigger phrase and leaves 'SEC. SCHOL.' in place.

rules.name: Spanish narrative marks a dialogue turn with a line-initial em dash (raya), not paired quotation marks
rules.scope: Spanish (and by extension French) narrative prose containing direct speech; the dialogue-inside-narrative case the brief specifically names for Cervantes.
rules.statement: Direct speech inside Spanish narrative opens with a line-initial em dash '—' rather than any paired quotation mark; when the narrator's own attribution tag interrupts a quote, the dash reappears around the tag and the quote resumes after it. A separate device, guillemets «», marks a different thing — a quoted WRITTEN document inside the narration, not spoken dialogue — including a continuation form where each subsequent paragraph of one long multi-paragraph quotation is re-prefixed with '»' rather than left unmarked.
rules.port: pending — a reference detector held under falsification; to be expressed as an organ primitive + table before the organ runs it
rules.counterexample: Both held-out originals exhibit the exact convention rule-11 describes -- direct speech opening a paragraph with a line-initial dash -- but this Gutenberg transcription house style renders it as plain ASCII double-hyphen '--' rather than Unicode em-dash U+2014, which the detector matches exclusively: Novelas ejemplares reads '--Si me dan cuatro cuartos, les cantaré un romance...' (U+2014 appears only 3 times in >1MB); Notre-Dame de Paris reads '--Sur mon âme, c'est vous, Joannes Frollo de Molendino!...' (U+2014 appears only twice, both inside Gutenberg's own English boilerplate, not the French text). The detector misses 100% of real instances in both files.

rules.name: Archive.org DjVu passthrough
rules.scope: Any live_priors .txt whose frontmatter cites an archive.org source_url ending in an item with a _djvu.txt derivative (this territory's 4 works confirmed; likely much of 11-multi-language and other archive.org-sourced collections).
rules.statement: For an archive.org-hosted scan, a corpus's plain-text copy that claims to carry archive.org's OCR forward should be byte-identical to that item's own <identifier>_djvu.txt after stripping a YAML frontmatter header and trailing end-of-file whitespace. Measured true for all 4 works in this territory: Ranke 1824, Ashworth 1887, Adams 1849, Stcherbatsky 1927. This means every OCR-era artifact found in this territory (long-s, combining-e umlauts, the doubled hyphen, the not-sign/soft-hyphen confusion, the marginalia splice, the bare page numbers) originates in archive.org's OWN OCR pass, not in a subsequent flattening step of our own fetch script — an important scope correction for anyone assuming 'our extraction damaged this'.
rules.port: pending — a reference detector held under falsification; to be expressed as an organ primitive + table before the organ runs it
rules.narrowedScope: The byte-for-byte comparison and its 'genuine damage' detection are sound and generalize cleanly to brand-new originals, but the check is brittle to three extremely common, content-preserving text transformations: (1) Unicode NFD normalization, (2) trimming only trailing per-line whitespace (which real editors do by default, and which would touch 62.6% of this document's own lines), and (3) a naively string-built frontmatter whose own field content happens to contain an unindented '---' line before the real closing delimiter, which makes stripFrontmatter truncate early and misclassify real frontmatter as body. All three make a truly undamaged copy report fired:false ('damage'). The rule should be read as 'byte-identical under NFC normalization and with frontmatter built by a real serializer', not literally byte-identical to whatever a downstream editor happens to produce.

rules.name: Fraktur double-hyphen marks line-end wraps
rules.scope: German-language, Fraktur-set text OCR'd by a pipeline that preserves U+2E17 (or, less consistently, ASCII '-') as the hyphen glyph — confirmed on Ranke 1824; refuted for the English translation of the identical content by the same pipeline.
rules.statement: Ranke 1824's German Fraktur OCR renders both compound-word hyphens and line-end word-division with the historical 'Doppelbindestrich' glyph U+2E17 (⸗), only rarely with plain ASCII '-'. Within the extracted text, being the LAST non-space character of an extracted line overwhelmingly marks a wrap point to strip-and-join, not a literal character: 2527 occurrences of ⸗, 95.33% line-final, vs. a computed per-document chance rate of only 2.06% (a document-relative null, not a hand-set threshold) — 46x above chance. Sampled strip-and-join reconstructions are clean words 23/40 times sampled (the rest fail only because the join-check itself is a coarse alphabetic-run proxy, not because the underlying join was wrong — e.g. 'Zuvoͤrderſt' scores clean, 'magyaN' does not because the sampler crossed a genuine sentence boundary). This gives S2's 'is this hyphen real' question a near-free answer for this document class, before falling back to S2's line-length-percentile geometry.

rules.name: Combining-e umlaut spelling coexists with precomposed umlauts
rules.scope: German Fraktur OCR from this archive.org pipeline; likely other historical-German-aware OCR profiles generally.
rules.statement: This OCR pass sometimes spells an umlauted vowel as the historical decomposed form VOWEL + U+0364 (COMBINING LATIN SMALL LETTER E — the little superscript 'e' Fraktur printing used before the two-dot diaeresis) instead of a precomposed ü/ä/ö, and BOTH spellings coexist in the very same document (4648 combining-e instances vs 2878 precomposed umlauts). 98.17% of combining-e instances sit directly after a/o/u (upper or lower case) — 9.6x the base rate of those six letters in the document overall (a computed, not assumed, null). rules.name: The document's own modal word-gap, not one space, is the baseline
rules.scope: Scanned-page OCR text broadly; measured to be real on some archive.org OCR outputs (Ashworth 1887, Adams 1849) and measurably ABSENT on others (Ranke 1824, Stcherbatsky 1927) and on a born-digital PDF extraction (Ashby) — i.e. a per-document property, never a pipeline-wide constant.
rules.statement: A text extractor's 'normal single word-gap' does not reliably render as one ASCII space. In a 400-line sample of Ashworth 1887, gaps of width 2 occur 2281/2899 times (78.7%) vs. a computed uniform-chance baseline of 16.7% for 6 observed widths — 4.7x above chance; Adams 1849 shows the same pattern even more strongly (84.7% at width 2, 11.0x above chance, with occasional 16-17-space runs from tabular/right-aligned material). Code that assumes '1 space = word boundary, 2+ = something special' will misfire constantly on these two documents. Crucially, the SAME general pipeline does NOT show this on Ranke 1824 or Stcherbatsky 1927 (both cleanly modal-1, 100% concentration) or on Ashby's born-digital pdftotext output (also modal-1) — so the correct engineering response is 'compute the mode per document', never 'assume a pipeline constant'.

rules.name: A marginal gloss gets spliced into the middle of a body sentence
rules.scope: Any page with a wide body column plus a narrow same-y-band outer-margin column, read by an OCR engine whose region/reading-order grouping does not separate the two — confirmed by hand and by coordinates on Ranke 1824 p.99; the coordinate-driven detector itself is NOT yet precise (see measured limitation).
rules.statement: Ranke 1824 sets marginal glosses in the right margin next to the body paragraph they summarize (e.g. 'Richtung Maximilians auf Italien.' beside the paragraph about Maximilian's ambitions toward Italy — confirmed visually on the fetched page image, pages/ranke_p140.jpg). Because the gloss and the body line it sits beside share a y-band, and archive.org's djvu.xml groups both into ONE reading-order PAGECOLUMN, the extracted text reads '...Botſchafter von Italien. „Alle Nictung Tage drohe Karl...' — 'Nictung' (OCR's misread of the gloss's first word, 'Richtung') is spliced directly between 'Alle' and 'Tage', which read as one continuous clause ('Alle Tage drohe Karl wieder zu kommen') with the intruder removed. A second, independent instance on the same page-pair (a bare page number '99' glued between two OCR-noise tokens and the paragraph's real first word 'Heier trafen ihn') confirms the mechanism is not a one-off.
rules.port: pending — a reference detector held under falsification; to be expressed as an organ primitive + table before the organ runs it
rules.narrowedScope: Fallback (text-only) mode: treat any fired:true as front-matter noise until proven otherwise -- on every new document tested, its 20 top candidates were title-case book/institution/translator names in preliminary matter, never a real mid-sentence splice. Strong (coordinate) mode: it does recover genuine splices, confirmed here on a second, independently-scanned copy of the very page the rule describes, but at very low precision (about 2 real hits among 34 same-page candidates), so a fired:true is a candidate list for human or further-CV review, never a confirmation, in either mode.

rules.name: pdftotext's only page marker is destroyed by a common cleanup step
rules.scope: Any pdftotext-default-mode extraction that is later 'cleaned up'; confirmed on Ashby 1956 (the only born-digital/pdftotext work in this territory).
rules.statement: Raw `pdftotext` default output's ONLY page-boundary marker is a bare U+000C (form feed), glued directly to the very first character of the next page's first line with NO preceding newline. rules.name: U+00AC (NOT SIGN) is this OCR's mis-mapped line-end soft hyphen
rules.scope: Stcherbatsky 1927's specific archive.org OCR run; the general mechanism (an off-by-one Latin-1 codepoint confusion, U+00AD SOFT HYPHEN -> U+00AC NOT SIGN) is a known class of encoding bug that could recur in any OCR/extraction pipeline, but is NOT observed in this territory's other 3 archive.org works.
rules.statement: 777 occurrences of '¬' (U+00AC, NOT SIGN) appear in Stcherbatsky 1927's OCR text, and ALL 777 (100%) fall as the last character of their extracted line. Stripping the mark and joining with the next line's leading letters reconstructs real English words every time sampled (38/40 sampled joins were clean; 'grati¬'+'tude'='gratitude', 'pheno¬'+'menal'='phenomenal', 'para¬'+'dise'='paradise', etc.) — this is this OCR pass's encoding of a line-end soft hyphen, not a logical-negation symbol, and a downstream reader that does not know this will leave truncated words glued to a stray '¬', or worse, corrupt meaning if the text is ever machine-interpreted. Plain ASCII '-' coexists in the SAME document (2597 occurrences) but is NOT interchangeable: only 9.59% of those are line-final — the two glyphs do different jobs in this one OCR output, not just noise scattered evenly across both.

rules.name: ASCII word/case regex has two distinct, script-dependent failure modes
rules.scope: Any line passed through eoreader7's medium.js first/last-word or capitalization logic. Splits into two regimes: (a) scripts with no A-Za-z codepoints at all (Chinese, Japanese, Arabic, Hebrew, Ethiopic, Lao, Devanagari, Cyrillic, native-alphabet Greek) -> EMPTY result; (b) Latin-based transliteration schemes carrying combining marks or precomposed accented letters outside A-Za-z (Sanskrit IAST, and by the same mechanism Vietnamese, diacritic Pinyin) -> WRONG/silently-truncated result, never empty. Does not fire on plain ASCII prose.
rules.statement: medium.js's `body.toLowerCase().replace(/[’']/g,'').match(/[a-z]+/g)` and `body.replace(/[^A-Za-z]/g,'')` (grepped at lines 43,46,55,143,180,183,185,197-198,205,210,220) silently mis-segment every line whose script isn't plain ASCII: no-Latin-letter scripts return an empty first/last word; Latin-with-diacritics schemes return a truncated one (stops at the first accented character). Neither failure raises an error.
rules.action: Route first/last-word, capitalization and shape detection through Intl.Segmenter (granularity: word) plus Unicode property escapes (\p{L}, \p{Lu}) instead of A-Za-z/a-z; treat combining-mark runs as part of the base letter, not a boundary.
rules.port: pending — a reference detector held under falsification; to be expressed as an organ primitive + table before the organ runs it
rules.counterexample: First Folio line "Strain'd with the variation of each soyle,": medium.js's real regex (which strips apostrophes before matching, by design) computes first="straind" -- correct per its own intended contraction handling. The detector's OWN ground-truth helper `realFirstToken` does not strip internal apostrophes, computes "strain'd", counts this as a mismatch, and the module's `fired` flag is computed from raw empty/wrong counts with no gating on `shape` at all -- so it fires on ordinary English contractions ("Balk'd", "Among'st", "Whil'st") and on stray non-prose lines (a bare Gutenberg URL), directly contradicting the rule's explicit "Does not fire on plain ASCII prose" claim.

rules.name: Quran ayah boundaries destroyed by bare-space array-join
rules.scope: Any text built by concatenating a per-item JSON API response (alquran.cloud, or any per-verse/per-ayah array API) with Array.join(' ') instead of one item per line. Confirmed for all 114 surahs in all 4 fetched live_priors tanzil-quran editions (ar quran-uthmani, en pickthall, en sahih, en yusufali) -- edition-independent, so the bug is in the shared fetch/join step, not the Arabic text specifically.

rules.name: Sof pasuq and maqaf are native verse/word markers, not editorial line breaks
rules.scope: Biblical Hebrew (Masoretic) text in any edition/source that has not had these characters stripped by a lossy pipeline. Verified on two independent sources (Sefaria API, OpenScriptures OSIS XML).
rules.statement: SOF PASUQ (׃, U+05C3) marks Hebrew Bible verse-end in the text itself, redundant with (not dependent on) any edition's line-splitting; MAQAF (־, U+05BE) marks prosodic word-joining. A byte reader can recover verse boundaries and joined-word units from these characters alone even with all newlines stripped.
rules.action: When parsing Biblical Hebrew, treat a maqaf-joined pair as one accentual word and locate verse ends via sof-pasuq rather than relying on the file's own line breaks.
rules.port: pending — a reference detector held under falsification; to be expressed as an organ primitive + table before the organ runs it
rules.counterexample: Genesis 1:5 (fresh Sefaria fetch) reads "...וֹם אֶחָֽד׃{פ}" -- sof pasuq (׃) is genuinely present at the true verse end. The detector's own `stripNoise` regex, `\{[סש]\}`, strips the closed-section marker {ס} and {ש} but NOT {פ} (peh, the OPEN-parashah marker -- arguably the more common of the two in Torah narrative, marking every 'day' break in the six days of creation). So `v.endsWith(SOF_PASUQ)` returns false for 6 of Genesis 1's 31 verses, dropping the measured rate from a true 100% to a measured 80.6%, which is enough to flip `fired` to false. A control run of the SAME current code against the original I Kings 1 grounding text also shows this bug already costing 2/53 verses there (96.2%, still just above threshold) -- so the bug was already latent in the grounding evidence, just not severe enough there to flip the verdict.

rules.name: wlc-tanakh pipeline drops maqaf and sof-pasuq corpus-wide
rules.scope: Text produced by joining OSIS-XML <w> element text with a plain space while discarding sibling <seg> elements. Confirmed specifically and corpus-wide for live_priors/14-holy-texts/wlc-tanakh/*.txt (38 files, derived from openscriptures/morphhb).
rules.statement: Every one of live_priors' 38 wlc-tanakh books (23,192 verse-tagged lines) has zero occurrences of maqaf (U+05BE) and zero of sof-pasuq (U+05C3), even though the underlying OSIS XML source carries both at a healthy rate (2,953 maqaf in Genesis alone) and a sibling pipeline on the same tradition (Sefaria) preserves both. Root cause, confirmed directly on the XML: these two marks live in <seg> siblings glued against <w> tags with no whitespace; a <w>-only, space-joined export silently converts a maqaf pair into two ordinary 'words' and drops the verse-final mark, while ordinary cantillation accents survive because they sit inside the <w> text node itself.
rules.action: Re-export wlc-tanakh from the OSIS XML including <seg type="x-maqqef"> (render as U+05BE with no surrounding space) and <seg type="x-sof-pasuq"> (render as U+05C3 with no preceding space), not just <w> text nodes.

rules.name: GRETIL sigla-then-text run-on is genre-specific and upstream of live_priors (re-grounds S8)
rules.scope: GRETIL's own 'plaintext transformation' files for terse/aphoristic Sanskrit genres (sutra literature) specifically. Does NOT apply to GRETIL's verse/epic transforms (Rigveda, Mahabharata), which keep one verse per physical line natively.
rules.statement: A GRETIL sigla token ('|| ps_1,1.1 ||', etc. -- edition abbreviation + citation address, not a closed word list) immediately followed by more non-whitespace text marks a place where per-unit line breaks are gone. Verified this is baked into GRETIL's OWN canonical plaintext file for Panini (sa_pANini-aSTAdhyAyI.txt: ~3,000 sutras packed onto one ~97,444-character line out of 60 total lines) and faithfully, byte-identically, copied by live_priors -- not something live_priors' own fetch step lost. GRETIL's Rigveda and Mahabharata-book-1 plaintext transforms do not show this: their live_priors line counts are near-identical to GRETIL's own (31,651 vs 31,627; 26,392 vs 26,385, gaps explained by live_priors' added YAML frontmatter).
rules.action: When re-splitting a terse-sutra GRETIL file, split on the sigla-token boundary itself (not on newlines, which don't exist at this granularity in the source); do not assume the same is needed for GRETIL verse/epic files.
rules.port: pending — a reference detector held under falsification; to be expressed as an organ primitive + table before the organ runs it
rules.counterexample: The fresh Jaimini original (gretil.sub.uni-goettingen.de/.../sa_jaimini-mImAMsAsUtra.txt) reads: "athāto dharmajijñāsā / jaim_1,1.1 /codanālakṣaṇo 'rtho dharmaḥ / jaim_1,1.2 /tasya nimittaparīṣṭiḥ / jaim_1,1.3 /..." -- textbook sigla-then-text run-on, arguably more extreme than the Panini grounding example (the closing delimiter itself touches the next word with zero whitespace). But GRETIL brackets this particular text's sigla with forward slashes ('/ jaim_1,1.1 /'), not pipes, while the detector's `SIGLA_TOKEN` regex hardcodes `\|\|?...\|?\|` (pipe-only), so it matches zero tokens on real, unambiguous run-on bytes.

rules.name: Doubled Ethiopic wordspace (፡፡) stands in for the dedicated full stop

rules.statement: Modern digitized Amharic/Tigrinya text marks a sentence end by doubling ETHIOPIC WORDSPACE (U+1361 U+1361, '፡፡') and does not reach for the dedicated ETHIOPIC FULL STOP (U+1362, '።') at all -- 0 occurrences of U+1362 across every file checked, vs a reliable doubled-U+1361 pattern in all of them.

rules.name: Zero-width space marks invisible syllable-wrap points in Lao, not word or clause boundaries
rules.scope: Lao web/digital text specifically verified; the same mechanism (UAX #14's SA 'Complex Context, South East Asian' line-break class) extends to Thai/Khmer/Myanmar but that extension was not independently checked this pass.
rules.statement: Lao has no native inter-word space (UAX #14 places it in line-break class SA, requiring dictionary/heuristic breaking). Live_priors' Lao children's books insert ZERO WIDTH SPACE (U+200B) between almost every syllable purely as a line-wrap opportunity -- never as a semantic boundary -- while genuine ASCII spaces mark real phrase gaps, and the text separately borrows ASCII '.' ',' '?' wholesale for punctuation the script has no native equivalent for.
rules.action: Strip/ignore U+200B when tokenizing Lao/Thai/Khmer/Myanmar text for word or clause boundaries; treat it purely as a rendering hint.
rules.port: pending — a reference detector held under falsification; to be expressed as an organ primitive + table before the organ runs it
rules.narrowedScope: Holds specifically for Global Digital Library/H5P-produced Lao book content. Does not extend to Thai Wikipedia (0 ZWSP, refuting the proposer's own flagged, previously-unverified 'extends to Thai' hypothesis) nor even to Lao Wikipedia typed through a different production path (0 ZWSP in the same language). rules.name: Arabic uses dedicated reversed comma/question mark but the plain ASCII full stop
rules.scope: Classical/Modern Standard Arabic from careful (Wikisource-quality) editions. Explicitly not a guarantee for mixed/messy sources -- see the in-corpus near-miss.
rules.statement: Arabic marks comma with U+060C (،) and question with U+061F (؟) as its own dedicated, mirrored Unicode characters, but -- unlike Urdu, which has U+06D4 (۔) -- reuses the plain ASCII full stop (U+002E) for sentence end. rules.name: Rendered/parsed MediaWiki HTML, not raw wikitext, is the root cause of page-UI-as-text (roots S4/S5)
rules.scope: Any MediaWiki-sourced (Wikisource, Wikipedia, ...) plaintext file, any language, wherever the fetch step used rendered/parsed HTML instead of raw wikitext. Confirmed on Chinese, Japanese and Arabic Wikisource pages in live_priors.
rules.statement: MediaWiki's raw wikitext marks every piece of non-body apparatus (license boxes, cross-reference boxes, navigation headers, edit-section affordances) with balanced {{template|args}} syntax, mechanically stripable with no CV or model. live_priors' matching .txt files show this apparatus already expanded into flowing, prose-shaped text with no surviving {{ }} anywhere -- proof the fetch consumed MediaWiki's rendered/parsed output (where the server pre-expands templates) rather than the source, and a plain HTML-to-text pass then flattened the resulting boxes.
rules.action: Re-fetch MediaWiki-sourced text via action=raw (or action=parse&prop=wikitext, never prop=text) and strip balanced {{...}} programmatically, instead of maintaining a per-language table of translated UI strings after the fact.
rules.port: pending — a reference detector held under falsification; to be expressed as an organ primitive + table before the organ runs it

rules.name: Kinsoku line-boundary prohibitions apply only to hard-wrapped CJK text

rules.name: Piped-wikilink target+label fusion
rules.scope: Any HTML->text extraction of MediaWiki-rendered content (Wikipedia/Wikisource/Wiktionary/Wikinews) that resolves a piped link [[Target|Label]] by concatenating the anchor's underlying data with its visible text and no separator. rules.statement: When [[Target|Label]] is rendered without its pipe/brackets, the flattened text shows a single unbroken run "TargetLabel" wherever Target's last word touches Label's first word with zero separator. Detect it without any external dictionary or hand-built word table: flag a long unbroken alphabetic token that splits into two halves which BOTH independently occur as free-standing whitespace-delimited words elsewhere in the SAME document (the document is its own vocabulary).
rules.port: pending — a reference detector held under falsification; to be expressed as an organ primitive + table before the organ runs it
rules.narrowedScope: Reliable only as a hint on HIGH piped-link-density, main-namespace wiki prose (true-positive rate 75-100% on fresh Wikipedia articles and a fresh Wiktionary entry, verified per-hit against the source wikitext). A caller cannot use fired:true alone; every hit must be checked against the source markup, which the detector does not do.

rules.name: Spaced-out inline citation brackets from DOM-node-join-with-space
rules.scope: Any DOM-walking HTML extractor that joins EVERY child text node with an inserted space rather than concatenating adjacent inline nodes with no separator. Most visible wherever <cite>/<ref> numbering renders as three separate text nodes.
rules.statement: MediaWiki's citation numbering emits three sibling text nodes with zero whitespace between them: "[", the number, "]". An extractor that inserts a space at every node boundary turns "Leibnitz,[1] who" into "Leibnitz, [ 1 ] who" — a strictly more specific and more diagnostic signature than generic entity debris (sw-html-entity-debris), because it also proves the extractor is spacing PER-NODE rather than per-real-word.

rules.narrowedScope: Holds wherever the DOM-walking HTML pipeline is actually used on content that has <ref>-numbered citations (both fresh EB1911 articles). Correctly absent from Wikipedia's real wikitext-regex pipeline, which never produces a rendered <sup>/<span> DOM at all, so the 'Any DOM-walking HTML extractor' framing describes a mechanism this corpus's Wikipedia fetch never invokes.

rules.scope: Wikinews "Shorts" (and similarly-shaped) compilation pages, where each compiled item independently carries its own licence/archival footer template.
rules.statement: A repeated boilerplate block in a compilation page is NOT automatically evidence of fetch-time subpage duplication (seed S7). Before concluding S7 applies, count an independent item-boundary signal (here: the count of "Sources" sub-headings, or [edit]-section markers) and compare it to the repeat count. If they match, the repetition is the SOURCE's own one-notice-per-item transclusion pattern.

rules.counterexample: Fetched the SOURCE WIKITEXT (not just rendered HTML) of both Wikinews Shorts pages. On the proposer's OWN Nov-13 grounding page, {{Archived-cc-2.5}} is transcluded exactly TWICE, both calls back-to-back at the very end of the page (after all 4 items' categories) -- NOT once per item. The '4 transclusions on a page with 4 items' the rule cites is the RENDERED notice-block count, which happens to equal that page's item count by coincidence. A fresh second page (Nov-18, 2008, the proposer's own held-out suggestion) reproduces the identical 'exactly two {{Archived-cc-2.5}} calls at the page end' pattern -- but with 3 real items, not 4, so notices(4) != items(3), and the detector's OWN countsMatch logic correctly flags this as 'unexplained by per-item count -- check for true fetch duplication (seed S7)', directly contradicting the 'source's own one-notice-per-item pattern' story on the only other page actually tested.

rules.name: Two-column layout + running head, read from tesseract box geometry alone
rules.scope: Any scanned reference-work page laid out in two (or more) columns with a running head, in any script — geometry is script-independent even when only English OCR is installed.
rules.statement: Cluster word bounding boxes by horizontal position: a genuine two-column page shows two populations of word left-x separated by a gap, each spanning most of the page height. A running head shows as a short text band confined to the very top of the page (roughly the top 6%) whose combined bounding box straddles both column midpoints. Neither test requires trusting the OCR'd TEXT, only the geometry — once this geometry is measured for one scan in a print run, it transfers to the rest of that print run without a fresh CV call.
rules.port: pending — a reference detector held under falsification; to be expressed as an organ primitive + table before the organ runs it
rules.narrowedScope: The running-head sub-detector HOLDS robustly, and is MORE general than the wikitext-based scan-furniture-noinclude detector: it correctly found the running head on Vol.16/p.319 (runningHeadGuess correctly includes 'LAW, W.—LAW' and '299') even though that page's differently-named {{rh|...}} template defeated the text-based detector above -- geometry doesn't care what the template was called. But the twoColumn sub-detector is unsound: it fires on a demonstrated single-column near-miss (Flatland p.28) because it only tests whether words split into two similarly-sized, similarly-tall groups around the page's horizontal midpoint -- a property that ANY full-width single column of justified prose satisfies trivially. Direct inspection of the word left-x histogram confirms Flatland p.28 has a smooth, gapless, continuous distribution across the full page width (no dip anywhere near the midpoint), unlike the genuine two-column EB1911 page (which shows a real, measurable density dip at its true gutter) -- a difference the coded algorithm never actually tests for.
rules.counterexample: flatland-p28.tsv (a genuine single-column novel page, confirmed via a full left-x histogram to have zero gap anywhere across its width): twoColumnLayout=true, leftColumnWordCount=162, rightColumnWordCount=157 -- both near-balanced and both spanning most of the page height, exactly the (insufficient) test the code performs.

rules.name: German federal statute Absatz numbers are literal in-prose "(N)" prefixes, not list markup — and this corpus's DE family renders them faithfully
rules.scope: German federal legislation as published on gesetze-im-internet.de (confirmed on the Grundgesetz; the same class="jnnorm"/jnhtml markup is used site-wide for all German federal statutes on that domain).
rules.statement: An Absatz's number is written as a literal "(N) " prefix inside the paragraph's own text — never a separate numbered-list element. A reader must look for this textual prefix, not for <ol>/<li> structure, to segment a German statute into Absätze. Checked against the actual source HTML and found faithfully preserved in this corpus with no artifact to report.
rules.port: pending — a reference detector held under falsification; to be expressed as an organ primitive + table before the organ runs it
rules.counterexample: legalize-de-TVG.md (Tarifvertragsgesetz), fetched fresh from the real mirror: contains 38 genuine '(N) ' inline Absatz-numbered paragraphs, but the detector returns fired=false / articleHeadingsFound=0, because its heading regex '^#{2,6}\s+(?:Art|§)\s*\d+[a-z]?\s*$' requires NOTHING after the section number, while TVG's real headings are '##### § 1 Inhalt und Form des Tarifvertrags' (number + descriptive title, the normal style for German statutes). legalize-de-URHG.md is a starker second instance: 559 genuine inline Absatz numbers, still fired=false. A sweep of ALL 15 pre-existing DE statutes already in the local corpus (legitimate held-out material) confirms this generalizes badly: 8 of 15 files (53%) score fired=false despite containing between 18 and 763 real inline '(N)' Absatz numbers each (BIMSCHG: 304, INSO: 763, MARKENG: 508, GMBHG: 279, KSCHG: 52, BURLG: 18, TVG: 38, URHG: 559) -- the grounding file GG.md (Grundgesetz) happens to use the atypical bare 'Art N' heading style with no title, which is why it alone matched. The underlying SOURCE-CONVENTION statement (inline '(N)' prefixes, never list markup) is not just uncontradicted but reconfirmed with far more instances than before -- only the detector's heading-gating logic is broken.

rules.name: USC subsections are sometimes unlabeled (indentation-only); never assume a full (a)(1)(A) address exists
rules.scope:
United States Code sections as published in the Office of the Law Revision Counsel's USLM XML (the authoritative structured original); applies wherever a section's clauses are USLM

without a child.
rules.statement: Some USC sections carry real, literal (a)/(1)/(A) labels in the XML (a citable statutory address exists); others — confirmed on 1 U.S.C. §1 — carry only role="listItem" class="indentN" paragraphs with NO stored label, so no (a)(1)(A) address exists for those clauses at all; any address for them is a reader's OWN positional convention, not the statute's. A correct downstream renderer must check for a literal label before assuming one, and must not fabricate fake letters/numbers for the unlabeled case.
rules.port: pending — a reference detector held under falsification; to be expressed as an organ primitive + table before the organ runs it
rules.narrowedScope: Fires reliably only for a genuine multi-clause USLM listItem enumeration rendered as markdown bullets (so far, only Title 1 §1's list of construction rules). It does NOT reliably signal 'this section lacks a citable address' more broadly: short single-sentence sections with no internal substructure (Title 4 §1 'Flag', Title 7 §1 'Short title' -- the proposer's own held-out 'expect fire' suggestions, chosen for being short and Title-1-like) produce NEITHER bullets nor labels at all, which the detector reports as the ambiguous 'neither pattern matched' bucket rather than as evidence of unlabeled structure. Worse, Title 4 §1's file was classified into the 'literal labels present' bucket only because of an incidental '(a)' appearing inside an unrelated quoted historical amendment note elsewhere in the file -- not because the operative section text itself has a real (a)(1)(A) structure.

rules.name: UDHR corpus's file-set shape is Unicode-Consortium-specific, not OHCHR's, despite every file's own OHCHR attribution
rules.scope: 06-government-legal/un-udhr/*.txt — all ~420 files in this family.
rules.statement: Every file's own 4-line header claims "Publisher: Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR)", but the FILE SET's shape — purely numeric identifiers for languages with no clean code (udhr-007 through udhr-071, several literally tagged "(und)" for undetermined), plus deliberate historical-orthography duplicates for one language (udhr-deu_1901 vs udhr-deu_1996; udhr-ron_1953/1993/2006) — is the fingerprint of the now-DISCONTINUED Unicode Consortium "UDHR in Unicode" project, confirmed live: unicode.org/udhr/ itself now states it stopped hosting the project in January 2024 and points to OHCHR instead. So this corpus's per-file OHCHR attribution describes the ORIGINAL rights-holder of the translations, one step removed from the numbering/packaging convention it actually mirrors.
rules.port: pending — a reference detector held under falsification; to be expressed as an organ primitive + table before the organ runs it
rules.narrowedScope: The practically important claim -- the file-set's numbering/duplicate-variant shape is NOT OHCHR's own scheme, and a reader must not cite OHCHR as its source -- holds and is reconfirmed on 4 fresh targets. But the specific attribution chain is more precise than stated: wooorm/udhr's own fresh README attributes its 'unicode' encodings not to unicode.org but to efele.net, which self-describes as the independent, STILL-ACTIVELY-MAINTAINED 'UDHR in XML' project (github.com/eric-muller/udhr, updates as recent as July 2026 confirmed live). The Unicode Consortium merely hosted a copy of this same Eric-Muller-maintained dataset for years under the name 'UDHR in Unicode' and stopped in January 2024 (re-confirmed live today on unicode.org/udhr) -- it was a downstream host of the numbering scheme, not its origin or maintainer, and the origin project is not 'now-discontinued' at all, only Unicode's mirror of it is.
